articles.title: When Your Parents Are Dying: Some of the Simplest, Most Difficult and Redemptive Life-Advice You’ll Ever Receive
articles.snippet: “Death makes human beings seem like very small containers that are packed so densely we can only be aware of a fraction of what’s inside us from moment to moment.” “Your children are not your children. They are the sons and daughters of Life’s longing for itself,” Kahlil Gibran wrote in his poignant verse on parenting . And yet we are, each of us, someone’s child — physiologically or psychologically or both — and they sing themselves through us as we sing ourselves into our longing for life, whether we like the melody or not. Like a Zen koan, this fact becomes utterly discomposing when you begin thinking deeply about the fundamental, layered realities beneath the mundane, even banal factuality of the fact. Parents — the very notion of them. The notion that you — this immensely complex totality of sinew and selfhood, this portable universe shimmering with a million ideas and passions and little ways of being-in-the-world that make you you — began as a glimmer in someone else’s eye, a set of chemical reactions that became molecules that became cells in someone else’s body before they constellated into you. The notion that so many dimensions of your personhood, so many of the givens you take for granted in making sense of the world, were forged by someone other than yourself (and possibly other than the body that begot the cells that became you) — someone who occupies, in the cosmogony of you, this strange and staggering position of arbiter between the existence and nonexistence of the particular you that you are. Kinship by Maria Popova. (Available as a print .) The doubly discomposing experience of what happens when that arbiter crosses the threshold of their own nonexistence is what Mary Gaitskill addresses in her thoughtful, tender contribution to Take My Advice: Letters to the Next Generation from People Who Know a Thing or Two ( public library ) — the wondrous 2002 anthology by artist and writer James L. Harmon, inspired by one of his own spiritual parents: Rilke and his timeless Letters to a Young Poet . Gaitskill writes: My advice here is very specific and practicable. It is advice I wish someone had given me as forcefully as I’m about to give it now: When your parents are dying, you should go be with them. You should spend as much time as you can. This may seem obvious; you would be surprised how difficult it can be. It is less difficult if you have a good relationship with the parent or, even if you don’t, if you’re old enough to have lost friends and to have seriously considered your own death. Even so, it may be more difficult than you think. With the sensitive caveat that there exist people “to whom this general directive does not apply” and her advice is not meant as a rebuke to those people, Gaitskill addresses those of us raised by fallible parents who, in one way or another, failed dreadfully at the deepest task of parenting — unconditional love: If you’re a young person who has had a bad relationship with your parent, it’s a nightmare of anger, confusion, and guilt. Even if you hate them, you may still not want to believe it’s happening… Even if your parents have been abusive, physically or emotionally, they are part of you in a way that goes beyond personality or even character. Maybe “beyond” isn’t the right word. They are part of you in a way that runs beneath the daily self. They have passed an essence to you. This essence may not be recognizable; your parents may have made its raw matter into something so different than what you have made of it that it seems you are nothing alike. That they have given you this essence may be no virtue of theirs — they may not even have chosen to do so. (It may not be biological either; all I say here I would say about adoptive as well as birth parents.) Art by Ekua Holmes from The Stuff of Stars by Marion Dane Bauer. Being with a dying parent, Gaitskill notes, is a way of honoring the fact — so basic yet so incomprehensible a fact — that they will soon be gone, and with them will go your experience of being their child in the way you have known, a fundamental way in which you have known yourself. At the heart of this dual recognition is “the hard truth that we know nothing about who we are or what our lives mean.” She writes: Nothing makes this plainer than being in the presence of a dying person for any length of time. Death makes human beings seem like very small containers that are packed so densely we can only be aware of a fraction of what’s inside us from moment to moment. Being in the presence of death can break you open, disgorging feelings that are deeper and more powerful than anything you thought you knew. If you have had a loving, clear relationship with your parent, this experience probably won’t be quite as wrenching. There may in fact be moments of pure tenderness, even exaltation. But you might still have to watch your parent appear to break, mentally and physically, disintegrating into something you can no longer recognize. In some ways this is terrible — many people find it absolutely so. There is another side to it, though: In witnessing this seeming breakage, we are glimpsing the part of our parents that doesn’t translate in human terms, that which we know nothing about, and which the human container is too small to give shape to. Art by Dorothy Lathrop , 1922. (Available as a print .) Because any emotional experience we have when facing another is always an emotional experience we have within, and about, ourselves — especially if that other gave rise to this self — facing this supraknowable quality is facing the limits of our own self-knowledge. Gaitskill writes: Knowing your feelings is hard too because there’s so much emotion, it’s hard to tell which is truest. Part of you might want to leave right away; part of you might want to stay forever. That’s why I advised that you stay “for as long as you can.” What that means will vary with each person, with the needs of the parent and the other relations. A day might

articles.title: What Is Your Refugium?
articles.snippet: For courage, says Bulgarian folk wisdom instructs, keep a horse chestnut in your pocket. Even as a child, I was mistrustful of superstition. But every autumn, I would pick up dozens of them from the sidewalks of Sofia and fill my pockets — not as a spell against fear but as an ode to joy. Conkers, as the English call them, spun me up in delight — shiny as mahogany, smooth as river stones, tiny planets from some other universe, the wonder-smitten eyes of some prehistoric creature. I didn’t know then that they are emblems of life’s irrepressible insistence on itself — miniature monuments to the stubborn creativity of survival. Illustration from Die Baume und Straucher des Waldes by by Gustav Hempel and Karl Wilhelm, 1889. Three million years ago, as the Ice Age was beginning to sink its cool blue fangs into the warm body of Earth, the widespread horse chestnut ( Aesculus hippocastanum ) began dying off, until only a small population remained, most of it sheltered in the gorges of Bulgaria’s mountains. There, in their sanctum of stone, the trees found themselves unable to attract pollinators during the slender three-week window of their flowering. This is the story of life — innovate or die: The horse chestnut evolved enormous white flower spikes with pink tips and a chemical hack to block the oxidation of polyphenols in the petal, which turns each flower brown and sheds it after pollination. For three whole weeks, the horse chestnut remains a bride in a gown of amazement, its crown an aria of perfect white blossoms that no bee can resist, all because there was a safe place in which to experiment with the possible. Illustration from American Medicinal Plants by Charles Frederick Millspaugh, 1887. That place, I learn from my poet friend Hannah Fries’s absolutely wonderful book A Forest Language , is called refugium . Hannah writes: When glaciers last crept down from the Arctic, 20,000 years ago, there were places where the icy fingers didn’t reach — mountaintops, hot springs, lowlands beyond the ice. There were pockets of green where things crawled and slithered and ate and mated, protected places where life went on, and from which life set forth again as the ice receded. Refugia. […] The gift of a refugium is time. It holds in its small cup of safety a promise for a new world to come. And it lends out to the living all the years, centuries, millennia it might take to finally find that world. Even in easier times, it is wise to tend the refuge. What is Earth, after all, but a momentary refugium in the inhospitable blackness of space? From a vantage point far beyond our grasping glows the blue-green dot, a brief and luminous memory in the mind of the universe. It is the memory of a place where a simple cell had the ambition to harness the energy of a star, and from it, the green wonder of leaves, the trunks rising up, bursting and blooming into the sky — all of life in the sweet, cool shade below. We too need them, these refugia that shelter us, that save us in the ice ages of life. Whatever your refugium may be — a place, a person, a practice, a poem — it is worth tending to with all the might and all the means you have. donating = loving For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a donation . articles.title: API credits benefit for eligible ChatGPT subscriptions
articles.snippet: API credits benefit for eligible ChatGPT subscriptions Earlier this month Anthropic announced a generous new benefit for their Max and Team subscriptions: $100, $200, and $500 per month subscribers would get the equivalent quantity of (expiring) credits to use with the Anthropic API. OpenAI have now launched pretty much exactly the same deal: if you have a $100, $200, or $500 subscription plan with them you now get that same quantity of credits to apply to one of your API organizations. I maintain subscriptions with both companies, so this is great news for me! I may even ship some public-facing demos now that the credits are already covered by my existing subscriptions. articles.title: White House makes Section 232 determination regarding foreign-made robots
articles.snippet: A Section 232 investigation by the secretary of commerce found that robotics imports pose a threat to U.S. national security and economic competitiveness. Source: Office of the White House Yesterday, U.S. President Donald J. Trump issued a proclamation stating that the secretary of commerce had submitted a Section 232 report about the national security effects of imports of robotics and industrial machinery, as well as related parts and components. “Based on the facts considered in that investigation, and taking into account the close relation of the economic welfare of the Nation to our national security and other relevant factors, see section 232(d) (19 U.S.C. 1862(d)), the Secretary found and advised me of his opinion that robotics, industrial machinery, and their components are being imported into the United States in such quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten to impair the national security of the United States,” stated the president. “Robotics and industrial machinery are critical to virtually all modern manufacturing processes, including for defense, commercial, and dual-use purposes,” he noted. “Furthermore, robotics and industrial machinery generate substantial economic value and support important economic activities, including approximately $7.1 trillion in shipments of manufactured goods in 2024 and the production of approximately $86 billion worth of equipment in 2024.” From mission-critical military and law-enforcement activities to critical infrastructure sectors such as agriculture , automotive , and electronics manufacturing , the U.S. government asserted that robots and related systems are vital to U.S. competitiveness. The value of such imported systems has grown over the past decade, and cybersecurity risks have also grown, according to the secretary of commerce. The Section 232 statement specifically cited “advanced robots — such as autonomous robots, humanoid and quadruped robots, and autonomous ground vehicles” as providing direct support to the U.S. military. While investments in U.S. robotics production capacity have increased, they are not sufficient to meet U.S. demand, said the president. He directed the secretary and the U.S. trade representative to “to enter into negotiations with trading partners to adjust imports of robotics, industrial machinery, and their components so that such imports will not threaten to impair the national security of the United States.” Will this Section 232 determination lead to tariffs on foreign made robots? With most of the major industrial automation providers based overseas, it remains to be seen how trade negotiations will go. The threat of geopolitical rival China is motivating policies such as this investigation and recent FCC restrictions . Submit your innovation now! Experts expect Section 232 negotiations before any tariffs Industry leaders and observers offered initial reactions: “As I articulated last week on [a] panel at the Arrowfly RoboBusiness conference in Santa Clara with respect to the FCC action, this is another strong signal of government support for those working on developing and expanding domestic supply chains for robots,” Brendan Schulman, vice president of policy and government relations at Boston Dynamics , posted to LinkedIn . He noted that the Special Competitive Studies Project ( SCSP ) Robotics Commission reached similar findings. “The next step for the federal government? Negotiations over the next six months with trading partners to adjust imports, and then further consideration of other trade policy measures,” added Schulman. “I am very pleased to see robotics gaining increasing attention and importance as one of the foundational technologies in need of broad, supportive policy action by the U.S. government. More to come, I’m sure!” Robert Little , former chief of robotics strategy at Novanta Inc., 2026 Joseph F. Engerlberger Robotics Award honoree , and business development advisor, concurred. “Robotics are critical for any country rebuilding its manufacturing. I’m thinking, what took so long to make this a priority?” he told The Robot Report . “Today, we still have limited industrial robot manufacturing in the U.S.,” said Little. “Already, FANUC , Teradyne Robotics , and Yaskawa have announced investments aimed at expanding U.S. robot manufacturing. I expect more to come, and I hope this new proclamation helps accelerate it.” “Yet, what concerns me most are the gaps in our domestic supply of components for robotics and industrial machines: sensors, actuators, precision gears, encoders and more,” he noted. “We need a much stronger U.S. supply base for these components. This is where we need the most help to strengthen America’s ability to manufacture.” The Section 232 investigation does not mean that tariffs will be immediate, added Ash Sharma , vice president of research and chief information officer at Interact Analysis . “This shouldn’t be read as a new robotics tariff today, but it is a clear indication of the direction of travel,” he said. “The U.S. government has explicitly identified its reliance on imported robotics and industrial machinery as a national security concern and is seeking to strengthen domestic production,” commented Sharma. “If tariffs, quotas or other trade measures follow, they could have meaningful implications for supplier competitiveness, pricing, and manufacturing localization in the U.S., potentially affecting not just finished robots, but [also] the components that go into them.” The Robot Report is expecting more responses that will be shared in subsequent coverage. Panelists discussed reshoring and policies such as the Section 232 investigation at RoboBusiness 2026. articles.title: 2026 Robotics Handbook looks at humanoids, AI, and design choices
articles.snippet: This year, The Robot Report continued to share developments in design, engineering, and deployment of commercial systems, but the pace of change has accelerated. This is due to advances in hardware, scale, and most of all, artificial intelligence. The 2026 Robotics Handbook curates some of the top trends in the space. As labor shortages drive demand for automation, markets become more knowledgeable about robots’ capabilities, and the systems themselves get easier to use, robotics adoption is growing. According to the International Federation of Robotics (IFR) and the Association for Advancing Automation (A3), both global and U.S. orders are climbing after a post-pandemic pause. This free download looks at the engineering challenges, component choices, and market opportunities for robotics. While humanoid robots are still in development and commercial trials, massive amounts of funding have led to stiff competition as big tech companies and emerging startups try different form factors and use cases. AI is the other prominent topic of 2026, as it changes how robots are designed, programmed, and managed. From large language models and vision-language-action models to world models, AI is already starting to make robots more autonomous, easier to use, and safer for people to interact with. However, the devil is in the details, as concerns around data, cybersecurity, and national sovereignty persist. What the 2026 Robotics Handbook features The 2026 Robotics Handbook also looks at advances in dexterous manipulation and spotlights an industry where automation is just getting started — construction. In this issue, you can learn about: The importance of cost, humans in the loop, and generalization versus specialization of manipulators with Plus One Robotics What effects integration, safety, and the desire for human-level abilities have on the pace of humanoid development as seen in Jabil’s collaboration with Apptronik A look at how Boston Dynamics has approached end effectors as it works to bring its Atlas humanoid robot to market The role of “virtual gyms” and simulation to accelerate AI for complex robot behaviors from SoftServe Why suction and soft grippers are better than either alone with Locus Robotics How Monumental determined that bricklaying was the place to start with automation for the construction industry Sponsors for the 2026 Robotics Handbook include DigiKey , All Motion , CS Hyde Co. , Boker’s Inc. , SIKO Products Inc. , and ElectroCraft . articles.title: Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models
articles.snippet: How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models. Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world. I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle. By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens"). Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request. Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat. This is continuous deployment turned up to 11: A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. Unshipped changes pile up, and every problem already in production lasts longer. The feedback slows down too. An agent can only keep a few hours of work in its head, so shipping faster than that actually helps it stay coherent. [...] We can roll back a broken change in 30 seconds, exactly where it's broken and nowhere else. When a monitor or a log alert fires, it starts or wakes an agent that owns the incident, and we break things on purpose to test that those recovery paths work. My eyebrows raised at least a dozen times reading this. I have trouble imagining this style of development working on software with higher stakes for when something goes wrong, but for a game this appears to be working surprisingly well. Jacob says that Fable 5 (and then 5.1) was the model that made this level of autonomy possible. Opus 5.5 doesn't quite hack it for them, and when they tried GPT-6 Astra to apply fixes from a security review everything stopped working: Every feature had been disabled and marked to be turned on again once the security fixes were done. Astra had gone through our whole product and made the insecure things secure by turning them off. These kinds of extreme experiments are why I'm excited about game development as a substrate for exploring the edges of what today's coding agents can do. Tags: game-design , ai , generative-ai , llms , claude , coding-agents , agentic-engineering , claude-mythos-fable

articles.title: What I learned about power from LBJ and Robert Moses
articles.snippet: Thanks to Max Farrens , who paired with me in writing the script for this video essay. I recently interviewed Robert Caro. He’s spent the last 50 years writing a four volume biography of Lyndon Johnson, and he spent another 7 years before that writing the biography of Robert Moses, the master builder of New York. His books are widely regarded as the best explorations of political power that have ever been written. They also happen to be literally my favorite books ever. Whenever I meet somebody new, one of the first questions they ask me is, “Who is it that you most want to interview that you haven’t yet?” And for six years, I’ve answered the question the same way: Robert Caro. I’ve spent so much time trying to make this interview happen: chasing his agent, calling his publisher, contacting the museums that have his archives, and even sending him handwritten letters. I finally got to sit down with him, and I’m very happy with how it turned out. It’ll be out this Friday. In the meantime, as I was preparing for the interview, and rereading these biographies, I wrote down the lessons they laid out about how to accumulate and use power. Robert Moses Robert Moses was the master builder of New York. He built more of the physical city than anyone before or since: the Triborough and Verrazano bridges, the Cross Bronx Expressway, Jones Beach, Lincoln Center, Shea Stadium, two giant power dams upstate, in addition to hundreds of parks and dozens of pools. Of the 899 miles of highways completed in New York State by 1964, Moses had built 672 of them. His projects collectively cost hundreds of billions of dollars in today’s money. For more than 30 years, Robert Moses was the most powerful person in New York (more powerful than any elected mayor or governor, despite not being elected to anything). How did he get and keep that much power? Exploits in law Part of the answer is that Moses wrote the laws that governed him. He was called ‘the best bill drafter in Albany,’ and he used that skill to write himself powers that the legislators voting on his bills didn’t know they were granting. The political genius of Robert Moses is perhaps best illustrated by his use of public authorities, which are government-created corporations that build city infrastructure. Public authorities sell bonds to pay for a specific project, say a new bridge. Once the bridge is built, the authority would charge drivers a toll until it had collected enough money to pay off its bonds. Then the authority would tear down the tollbooths, hand the bridge over to the city, and go out of existence. At least, that was the idea. And that’s what Albany assumed would happen when the New York State Legislature approved the Triborough Bridge Authority Act of 1933, whose final version included - buried within pages and pages of legalese - a few seemingly minor alterations drafted by Robert Moses. Section 1 clearly stated that the authority would dissolve once the bonds were paid off. And since the bonds could run at most 40 years (and the revenues from the bridge would pay back the initial cost far sooner), it seemed like the authority had a clear, built-in expiration date. However, in a subsection of Section 9, Moses added a single sentence that said the Authority could “from time to time” pay off its old bonds by issuing new ones. And those new ones could be “for any other corporate purpose.” So just before the original bonds were about to expire, the authority now had the right to issue a totally fresh 40 year note, for a potentially totally different use. And what could the Authority build with all that money? The original act let it build two bridges and their “approaches.” Moses’ amendments also gave this authority the right to build “connecting” roads and “facilities not inconsistent with the use of the project”. These rights, when interpreted as creatively as Moses intended to, would allow Moses to alter most of the roads, parks, and housing in New York - for if a road connected to a road which connected to a road which connected to the bridge, or if a park lay along the road that connected to the road that connected to the road that connected to the bridge, surely the Triborough Authority was entitled to improve and change it. All this construction could be financed by the bridges’ enormous toll revenues and the right of the Triborough Authority to borrow against them. To give some perspective, in 1946, the entire New York City government could only borrow $150 million before hitting its legal debt limit. That very same year, Triborough could borrow $360 million. So Moses’ bridge authority had access to more than double the amount of money as the largest city in America. But what if a future governor or mayor eventually learned about all the power and revenue that had been delegated to this authority, and decided to claw back? Moses had planned for that too, and his solution was so clever that no lawyer or lawmaker in Albany saw it coming. The US Constitution says that no state shall make “any … Law impairing the Obligation of Contracts” entered into by a government entity. A bond issued by a public authority is such a contract. Moses snuck a clause into the law that allowed him to add into those bond contracts “any other matters, of like or different character, which in any way affect the security or protection of the bonds”. These “matters” included whether Triborough could charge tolls for however long they wanted, and whether they would get to keep the surplus thus generated. That is to say, Moses could now entrench his powers simply by writing them into the bonds he issued. From the moment the bonds were sold, those powers could no longer be revoked by the Legislature, the governor, or the mayor - by anything, in fact, short of a Constitutional Convention. The powers that Moses now had were guaranteed for the bonds’ entire lifetime - a lifetime which could always be extended simply by refinancing. So, with just a few minor tweaks

articles.title: At the Money: Preparing for a Career in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
articles.snippet: At The Money: Preparing for a Career During in Age of Artificial Intelligence (October 29, 2026) Full transcript below . ~~~ About this week’s guest: Nitin Nohria is former Dean of the Harvard Business School , where he is still a professor. He is the author of The CEO: The Role, the Reality, the Responsibility For more info, see: Professional Bio LinkedIn Previous At the Money ~~~ Find all of the previous At the Money episodes here , and in the MiB feed on Apple Podcasts , YouTube , Spotify , and Bloomberg . And find the entire musical playlist of all the songs I have used on At the Money on Spotify Nitin Nohria: Preparing for a Career in the Age of AI Barry Ritholtz in conversation with Nitin Nohria, former dean of Harvard Business School and author of The CEO: The Role, the Reality, and the Responsibility. Bloomberg Radio. BARRY RITHOLTZ: In the age of artificial intelligence, how should students prepare for this job market? Let’s bring in Harvard Professor Nitin Nohria. He’s former dean of the Harvard Business School. His new book is The CEO: The Role, the Reality, and the Responsibility. He’s also executive chairman at Thrive Capital, which is the venture firm run by Joshua Kushner. So let’s start with AI. If artificial intelligence is attacking that entry rung of the career ladder, how should recent college grads build the skills and judgment that used to come from those entry-level jobs? NITIN NOHRIA: First, students should continue to use their time during their education to be even more determined to cultivate critical thinking — the capacity to interrogate themselves. When I teach cases now, one thing I’ve started to do is to ask students, “Tell me what AI said about this case.” Actually, not just tell me — read to me what your AI agent said to you about this case. Because I want them to know you can use these tools. In fact, you’ll be required to use these tools when you get to work. NITIN NOHRIA: And then I ask them the second question: What did you agree with? What did you disagree with? What further questions did you ask to get your thinking to be improved? I think this form of critical reasoning — where we rely upon AI to inform ourselves, but then we interrogate it deeply, and we learn how to think alongside it — this is a capability that they will be required to have, and I think the best students will prepare themselves this way. BARRY RITHOLTZ: So your preference is, rather than just become a very inch-wide, mile-deep domain expert, really have the broad meta-skills — critical reading, critical thinking, and a more intelligent form of learning and working with AI. Is that the takeaway? NITIN NOHRIA: I think so. My view increasingly is that you should think of AI very much like in the Marvel comics. Each person can develop their own superpower. You don’t need a Marvel suit; AI becomes the equivalent of your Marvel suit. But you have to tune it to yourself, right? It’s not like all Marvel heroes have the same superpowers. You will develop your own superpowers, and that’ll be your distinctive edge. How you use this extraordinary capacity to distinguish yourself, to make yourself special — that will be the new edge that people will have to find. BARRY RITHOLTZ: So, undergraduate: does the major a student takes really matter? We saw such a push towards STEM, but now it seems a lot of those technical skills are getting commoditized. How should a student be thinking about what they should be studying, how they develop judgment and communication skills? How important is the major? NITIN NOHRIA: In the same metaphor that I used — you have to find what your unique Marvel superpower is — expertise could be one of them. It is not the case that expertise disappears. If you end up being the person who has dug deep into computer science, and you can therefore answer questions about the right way to program using AI, about the right way to create safety — all of the questions that are now being worked on by the leading researchers at the top labs — that’s not something that I, who doesn’t have that same level of intuition, experience, and expertise, will be able to do. NITIN NOHRIA: For others, it may be writing. For others, it may be history. So I do think that a major will continue to be important. But then there will be people who take interdisciplinary majors — like Social Studies at Harvard — who say, “I’m not going to differentiate myself on expertise, because that will be for some people. I’m going to be the generalist.” And I think that being a generalist is going to be deeply important in this world too. BARRY RITHOLTZ: Yeah, no doubt. So let’s talk about that first job, which, when I was coming up, was described as the all-important first job. Is that still the case? Should people think about that first gig out of college as something that’s a little bit of an experiment, to figure out what they like and what they’re good at? Or should it be a commitment to the company, to the industry, to their bosses — just jump in with both feet? Or somewhere in between? NITIN NOHRIA: In my experience, having taught for now almost 40 years — I teach mostly business school students, who are graduate students, but I’ve also had interaction with lots of undergraduate students — I find that students are of two types. There are people who, somewhere very early in their life, know exactly what their life’s mission is. I’ve always said to those people: get on with it. Find a place, commit, dig deep, because you already know what you want to do. Don’t waste time flitting around running experiments. The experiment of your life is already known. Now you have to find a way to deliver on it. NITIN NOHRIA: And there are other people — and I will put myself in that category — who didn’t have a clue about what I wanted to do when I joined an undergraduate institution. Didn’t even have a clue when I went to graduate school, and had to discover through experimentation what it was that I was going to be go

articles.title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
articles.snippet: Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs. Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities. Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem. Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/relay-video-v14-1080p.mp4 Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation. David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes. Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection. Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries. Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Turbine-Lab-RTX-and-What-If-under-10MB-1.mp4 Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator. The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error. The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing. Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene ( ovstage ), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments. Build Simulation Scenes With Open Source SimReady Assets https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/kitchen_final_blog_with_music.mp4 With SimReady Central Library, announced at GTC Berlin , developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows. Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments. For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment. Find assets in SimReady Central Library , and learn how to contribute . Stress-Test a Warehouse Simulation at Scale https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infra-scale-demo-20260914_144614-Meeting-Recording.mp4 A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene. When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns. Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling. With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements. Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve. Start building with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries . Test Robot Control for Flexible Cable Routing https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/scurve_rl_vs_astra_side_by_side.mp4 In electronics assembly, a robot may need to position a flexible cable around components before plugging it into a port. The cable bends as the robot moves it, and the connector must line up precisely to fit. Oyindamola Omotuyi, robotics technical marketing manager at NVIDIA, directed Astra to build a robot simulation using NVIDIA Isaac Lab , Newton physics and Omniverse rendering with a Robotiq gripper handling the cable. articles.title: Can Frontier Models See Past a Decoy? Elorian Tests Visual Reasoning
articles.snippet: This month Elorian launched its first visual reasoning model , Glimpse . It’s being promoted as “a new category of visual thinking model: a system that reasons about the physical world from what it sees.” View post on X ↗ So how does Glimpse compare to both frontier models and world models in vision tests? A new benchmark called DecoyCount , co-released by Elorian, provides some answers. We quizzed CEO Andrew Dai on the benchmark, and also talked about Elorian’s positioning in a crowded models landscape. DecoyCount results Elorian emerged from stealth in April with $55 million in seed funding , co-led by Striker Venture Partners, Menlo Ventures and Altimeter Capital. Now, in partnership with AI data company Mercor , Elorian is announcing the DecoyCount benchmark, which tests whether language models genuinely count objects or rely on visual shortcuts and substitution heuristics. According to a paper accompanying the release , frontier models scored below 50% accuracy on DecoyCount — the highest was GPT-6 Astra, with 43.17%. Elorian’s new model isn’t mentioned in the paper, but Dai told us that Glimpse scored 50.48% in an internal test. Regarding the frontier models, the paper concludes that “stronger general reasoning does not by itself generalize to aligned visual reasoning.” How the benchmark works: “DecoyCount exposes interpretable counting failures across seven mechanisms.” To make sure it was a like-for-like comparison with the frontier models, we asked whether the paper’s evaluation images were withheld from Glimpse’s training? “The evaluation images and text were withheld from our training, and our contamination check found no overlap in the training data checked,” Dai replied, via email. “Without any cues, Glimpse scored 50.48% on the 1,660 DecoyCount items, making it the only model in the comparison to clear 50%. The closest was GPT-6 Astra at 43.17%, about 7 points behind, and Gemini-3.8-flash scored 32.71% while Qwen3.8-max scored 28.31%, and Claude-Fable-5.1 came in at 25.22%.” Dai did note that Glimpse’s results “come from a single run of the model on its own, without an agent or tool harness,” whereas the six models from the paper were each averaged across three runs under their reported settings. DecoyCount benchmark results for frontier models over 3 runs each. But what exactly is DecoyCount revealing that existing model benchmarks miss? According to Dai, it tests both vision and reasoning together — which most benchmarks elide. “If a person sees an apple in front of a mirror, we know that there’s just one apple and it’s being reflected. But a model might miss the apple entirely (a vision problem) or count the apple and its reflection as two (a reasoning problem). But most benchmarks that test for this error only check the final number, so both mistakes are treated the same way, which is an issue if you want to fix the root problem and can’t tell if it’s an issue of vision or judgement. ” Frontier Model Comparison in DecoyCount paper What is visual thinking exactly? Andrew Dai isn’t a Johnny-come-lately on the AI scene. In 2015, while working at Google, he co-authored a paper entitled Semi-supervised sequence learning . In this paper, Dai and his then colleague Quoc Le demonstrated an early version of the pretrain-then-fine-tune approach later adopted in large language models. Over the decade that followed, Dai worked for Google DeepMind on GLaM MoE, PaLM 2 and then Gemini. Dai only left Google this year, in order to co-found Elorian. Part of his motivation was to push the boundaries of what vision models can do. His approach, he explained to Latent Space, is based on a concept in human psychology called visual thinking . When most people “think about spatial problems or visual problems,” he explained, “they visualize the problem [by] generating images and editing images in their mind.” He gave an example of buying a sofa and mentally picturing what it will look like in your living room. A conceptual visual reasoning loop There’s also manipulating an image in your mind ; for example if you’re counting people around a table, you might mentally “cross them off one by one,” Dai said. This is what Elorian aims to do in its models: teach them visual thinking “that involves generation and editing images as part of the reasoning trace, along with language.” The key point is that image generation isn’t just an output for a vision model — the generated or edited image is part of a chain of reasoning. How is Elorian different from World Models? Visual reasoning is still a work in progress, but there have been some impressive releases this year in “world models” — where vision is a key component. Two that stand out are World Labs’ Atlas in September (the company was subsequently acquired by AMD ) and Google’s just released Genie 4 . When World Labs announced Atlas , it was described as an “omni world model for spatial intelligence.” But what Atlas enables — basically a 3D simulation of a world — isn’t the same as visual reasoning. According to Dai, world models enable “direct action on a world,” whereas Elorian is more focused on what he calls “indirect action.” By that he means using visual reasoning to inform a decision or workflow (what Glimpse does) , rather than building simulated environments that allow navigation and manipulation (what Atlas does). As an example, you might use visual reasoning to decide whether to reject a user-contributed video for violating a policy. “You don't need a 3D rendering to do that,” said Dai. Applications for visual reasoning Other business opportunities for Elorian include robotics, engineering, and defense applications. Dai added that architects need to regularly check building codes and compliance — an ideal task for a vision reasoning model. Traditional Chinese martial arts meet mechanical prosthetics, industrial ruins and rock music in a distinctive kungfupunk world. Ultimate members can wield GeForce RTX 5080-class performance in the cloud across PCs, Macs, handhelds, mobile devices, browsers, compatible TVs and more. GeForce NOW handles the game’s downloads and storage, leaving more time for the next clash. Soul’s clock is ticking, but the download bar doesn’t have to. Once available, members can sign in to their GeForce NOW account and head to the Account Portal to redeem. Mark the calendar and gather the party — launch week is approaching. Familiar favorites have a few new tricks, too: Mod.io support is now available directly in game for Cyberpunk 2077 and The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Remastered , bringing more ways to make Night City and the Continent feel different. articles.title: An Interview with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar About the AI Religious War
articles.snippet: Listen to this post: Good morning, Today’s Stratechery Interview is with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar . Sankar has worked at Palantir for 20 years, and has taken on an increasingly visible role as public intellectual, including authoring the book Mobilize , an exhortation “To Reboot the American Industrial Base and Stop World War III”. I previously interviewed Sankar in June 2023 . That interview is a great place to start in terms of understanding Palantir, which we mostly discuss in this interview in the context of AI. To that end, in this interview we discuss why Sankar thinks the industry is insufficiently focused on AI diffusion, why companies focused on the top-line have more success adopting AI, and why he is frustrated at the labs refusal to take a systems engineering approach to AI safety. Then we discuss what Palantir has learned from AI, how companies can preserve alpha instead of the median, and whether or not we need more models. Sankar also explains exactly what a forward-deployed engineer is, why tech is in a religious war, and his retrospective on Anthropic’s battle with the U.S. government. This Interview is presented by Stripe, the economic infrastructure of AI, and for Stratechery itself. As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player. On to the Interview: An Interview with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar About the AI Religious War This interview is lightly edited for clarity. Topics: Diffusing Intelligence | Top Line vs. Bottom Line | Safety and Systems Engineering | Palantir’s AI Lessons | Alpha vs. Beta | Model Questions | Forward-Deployed Engineering | Anthropic vs. the U.S. Government | AI Religion Background Shyam Sankar, welcome back to Stratechery. SS: Ben, thanks for having me back. Well, the last time we talked was in conjunction with Ted Mabrey , the head of Palantir Commercial. As is usually the case with dual interviews, we got right down to business — and I do have to say, I do a lot of interviews where I usually kind of know where I want to go, but that one was super helpful to me in understanding Palantir and thinking about AI generally . But before we get into that, we never got to do my traditional background questions — where you came from, how you got to where you are. So for you, do we start in Orlando, in Lagos, or in India? SS: At least Lagos. My father, in his early 20s, moved to Lagos and built one of the first pharmaceutical manufacturing facilities in all of Africa. He set up this whole life there for the better part of ten years. I was born in India, but really I grew up until I was three in Lagos. And then there was this horrible armed robbery that happened at the house — they decapitated the dog, pistol-whipped my father, and threatened my mother. So we left all of our earthly possessions behind and started over again in Orlando, which ended up being a truly phenomenal place to grow up. The profound optimism of Disney World, the shadow of the Space Coast , seeing shuttle launches in elementary school, running into your courtyard filled with this sense of optimism about how technology will inevitably lead to a better world — which, if you fast-forward twenty years from the ’80s, I think kids were fed a very different diet of Terminator and “ nature always finds a way “, “How dare man try to do anything that creates progress?”, so that’s really where it started. Is that actually the ultimate example of man overcoming nature — not the space shuttle, but in fact Disney World? SS: (laughing) That’s true! The fact that millions of people go there every year, to the middle of the swamp — and it’s fantastic, a lot of fun. What does meritocracy mean to you? I was reading the recent profile of you in Colossus , and it opened with [Palantir CEO] Alex Karp’s statements in that regard, but it was put in the context of you growing up in Orlando, taking an entrance exam to go to Trinity High School, and how that launched you into what you became. Is that a sentiment from Alex, is it from you, or what’s your take? SS: It’s a sentiment for both of us, for different reasons. We’re both kind of acquired tastes, in many ways, and living in a world that judges you by the fruits you bear, rather than any dimension you have no control over, is obviously a better world to live in. I think it’s a precondition to the American Dream. I was going to ask you that. Because you have this background — born in India, originally living in Lagos, come to America. What does being an American mean to you? Is that the same question, or is there some tension between those two things? SS: They overlap profoundly. Being an American is this profound belief in your own human agency, and the community you’re in, and the ability to create a more perfect union — the recognition, the ability to hold the contradiction, that not everything is perfect today but it’s incumbent on us to make it better. That may sound a little Pollyannish and even corny, but that doesn’t exist anywhere else. Everywhere else, people are profoundly cynical — things are the way they are — and there’s a very thin line between cynicism and nihilism, and you kind of give up on everything. That’s the death spiral, that’s how you get the Dark Ages. After university and graduate school, you worked on Xoom, on remittances — and then you go to work for Palantir. SS: Xoom with an X. Xoom with an X, that’s right. Not the Zoom with a Z — which maybe I shouldn’t be talking to, since you’re now an executive at Palantir using Zoom with a Z, but that’s another discussion. You worked on Xoom and remittances, then Palantir, working on national security, arguing for building our homegrown industrial base. There’s an argument there that — to take a paradox that’s maybe unfair — how do you go from a career focused on sending money out of America to being an advocate for money here in America, rebuilding our capital bas

articles.title: Explaining funny
articles.snippet: This is one of the most famous comedy bits of all time: But why is it funny? The disconnect between experiencing it and explaining it represents one of the challenges of teaching. It’s also at the heart of leadership, marketing and culture. Design, good taste, genre, communication style–these are all human endeavors that inform our days, but most of the time, we’re at a loss to explain them. Abbott and Costello are avatars, approachable and relatable to their audience. You can see yourself as one or the other, depending on the moment. They’ve plotted an intricate dialogue, one that builds on itself, gaining traction and increasing tension as it goes. And as each expresses their frustration with the situation (and to a degree, with each other), it’s easy to put ourselves in their shoes. We’ve never been in this exact situation, but we’ve all experienced a moment like this. Most of us are in on the joke as we watch it. We know it’s a joke, and we understand early on the nature of the wordplay. So much so that the sketch itself becomes an icon, one that others are based on, sometimes with great fidelity: Funny even before the reign of U2. So iconic that it’s now a three-word shorthand. We can have the same discussion about your logo. Or why your book cover is less than it could be. When someone is designing a bridge, we don’t have to wonder if the engineer “gets it.” The metrics are obvious and easily measured. We have precise words and numbers that are external to our own experience and the zeitgeist, and whether a person or a machine does the calculations, it works or it doesn’t. But much of the rest of the human experience is often too layered and nuanced to be reduced to a simple formula. We need to notice enough and engage enough to get it. That’s what Heinlein was talking about when he coined the 60s term grok . When a municipality sets aside the resources to build a ‘signature’ bridge, their own Golden Gate, there’s often a conflict. Not just disagreement about the need for something more than the utility of moving across the river, but also understanding what beautiful and important even looks like. Some people don’t get it. Saying “that’s not funny,” or “I think it’s ugly,” is easy. The difficult work is acknowledging that someone else might disagree. Human emotions require a viewer, not just a creator. The funny, the beauty, the elegance: they happen for someone, in their experience. “That’s not beautiful,” is not the same as, “I don’t think that’s beautiful.” I don’t have to explain a joke or a sculpture or a logo. But I do have to know enough to imagine that someone else is going to get it. We can choose to care enough to figure out why someone gets something we don’t, and imagine what it might take to create something human enough that others will care about it. There’s no algorithm, which is part of the point.

articles.title: [AINews] Gemini 4 Carbon tops leaderboards, launches for cyber defenders
articles.snippet: It’s a good thing we published our Opus 5.5 podcast calling it the world’s best model before today’s launch. In a very pleasant surprise, Gemini announced Carbon , a newer frontier model than the 3 week old Argon , with fantastic benchmarks: Taking it to the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis consolidated benchmark, putting GDM in the lead for possibly the first time in AAII history: View post on X ↗ sd AI News for 10/27/2026-10/28/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap Gemini 4 Carbon Tops Independent Leaderboards, with Access Limited to Cyber Defenders Launch : Google DeepMind announced Gemini 4 Carbon two weeks after Argon. It is positioned as state of the art on cybersecurity and long-horizon tasks ( @sundarpichai , @GoogleDeepMind ). Claimed cyber results : 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro for vulnerability finding, 54.8% on ExploitGym for exploitation and 71.0% on CWE-bench for patching ( @sundarpichai ). Availability : Carbon first goes to trusted cyber defenders through the Fairwind Program, with wider developer access promised "as soon as possible" ( @GoogleAI ). Pricing : Phil Schmid quotes $2/$10 per million input/output tokens with an asterisk ( @_philschmid ). Artificial Analysis lists $4/$20 standard pricing with a 50% launch discount that has no end date. Cached input costs $0.20 per million tokens ( @ArtificialAnlys ). Specs : The model has a 1M-token context window and 1M max output. Inputs are text, image, video and speech; output is text ( @ValsAI ). Safety claims (Google) : Successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 fell to 0.0%, and cheating attempts fell to 0.4%. Unsupported claims are down about 2x versus Argon. Overreach fell 26% and under-service fell 29% ( @OfficialLoganK ). Artificial Analysis : Carbon is #1 on Intelligence Index v5 with a score of 59. It leads 4 of the 9 index evals: HLE-Diamond, TB-Science, AA-Omniscience and AutomationBench ( @ArtificialAnlys ). Coding : On the Coding Agent Index, Carbon scores 59 using Antigravity CLI, versus 62 for Claude Code with Opus 5.5 [max]. It scores 51% on FrontierCode v1.1, versus 56% for Opus. Knowledge work : Carbon reaches 1609 Elo on AA-Briefcase, up 126 points from Argon. It still trails Grok 4.7, Muse Wonder and Kimi K3.1 Pro (1678). Cost : Carbon costs $7.76 per index task, versus $10.04 for Opus 5.5 and $6.25 for GPT-6 Astra. It uses 123k output tokens per task, 29% fewer than Opus. Hallucination : Carbon leads Omniscience with 54. Its hallucination rate rose from Argon's 4% to 11%, which is still the second lowest measured. Opus 5.5 and Astra are both at 50%. Other independent evals : Arena : Carbon is #1 in Text Arena (1528), #2 in Agent Arena at a $1.80 median cost per task, and #4 in Code Arena: WebDev (1768) ( @arena ). Arena attributes the gains over Argon to more praise, more confirmed successes and better steerability ( @arena ). Vals : Carbon is #2 on the Vals Index and #1 on the Finance Index and Legal Research Benchmark. It produces 64% more output tokens than Argon, mostly on finance, tax and legal tasks ( @ValsAI , tokens ). Coding benchmarks : Carbon scores 61.2% on FrontierSWE, behind GPT-6 Astra (65.5), Opus 5.5 (62.3) and Sonnet 5.5 (61.9) ( @ProximalHQ ). It sets a narrow state of the art of 9.6% on SWE-sweep ( @KLieret ). Andon Labs : Carbon is #1 on Vending-Bench 2 ( @andonlabs ). It is also #1 on Blueprint-Bench 2, where it ties the human baseline for 3D spatial understanding ( @andonlabs ). Caveats and reactions : Harness : The coding-agent results were measured in Antigravity CLI, so results in other harnesses are untested ( @Yuchenj_UW ). Hallucination risk : Some users are concerned about hallucination in cyber use ( @scaling01 ). Lab gap : scaling01 thinks Google remains about two months behind the next OpenAI and Anthropic releases ( @scaling01 ). RSI framing : On the earnings call, Sundar Pichai said AI is increasing training and launch velocity. He expects "continued acceleration because of RSI" over the next twelve months ( @AndrewCurran_ ). Unconfirmed : Claims of a stronger unreleased Gemini model are not confirmed ( @kimmonismus ). Internal workflow : A Gemini engineer describes overnight agent loops and swarms that inspect RL data. In that workflow, launches now feel like "periodic checkpoints" ( @zhangqiaorjc ). Leaderboard Resets and Benchmark Integrity AA Intelligence Index v5 : The rebuilt index runs 60% on private tests ( @TheRundownAI ). Ranking before Carbon : Opus 5.5 scored 58, followed by GPT-6 Astra (57), GPT-6.1 Sol (55), Sonnet 5.5 (54) and GPT-6.1 Terra (51). Open models : Kimi K3.1 Pro fell from 55 to 46. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM-5.3 both score 32, below Claude Haiku 5.5 at 36. China–US gap : scaling01 puts the gap at about 3.3 months on the AA Progress Index ( @scaling01 ). FrontierCode 2.0 mystery model : Cognition data includes a hidden "Obsidian 3" scoring 46.8%, versus 45.5% for Opus 5.5. Because it runs in the claude-code harness, some speculate it is Fable 5.5; this is unconfirmed ( @kimmonismus ). DeepSeek correction : scaling01 corrected an earlier identification and said Artificial Analysis shows DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 at about 28% ( @scaling01 ). Mixed sources : teortaxes notes that Cognition's chart mixed model-card scores with independently measured ones ( @teortaxesTex ). Cost comparisons are fragile : teortaxes argues that list-price comparisons of Haiku 5.5 and V4.1-1017 distort real costs. The comparison uses DeepSeek's peak pricing, ignores Haiku's long-context surcharge and does not reflect Haiku's roughly 2x output tokens ( @teortaxesTex ). "Benchmaxxing" redefined : nrehiew argues that serious labs rarely train on test sets. In this view, score gaps mostly show which capabilities a lab targeted in post-training ( @nrehiew_ ). New evals : Gym-Anything-RT

articles.title: AGIBOT introduces Worken to measure robot productivity at AGIBOT Innovation Day 2026
articles.snippet: Peng Zhihui, president, CTO, and director of AGIBOT, introduces Worken at AGIBOT Innovation Day 2026. Source: AGIBOT AGIBOT today introduced Worken, a proposed framework for measuring the productivity of robots in real-world environments, at AGIBOT Innovation Day 2026 in Shanghai. Combining the words “Work” and “Token,” the concept seeks to shift attention beyond the number of robots manufactured or deployed toward how much useful work they can perform autonomously and consistently. The company also unveiled AHA3, its integrated “three intelligences in one” hardware platform, and highlighted advances in its AGILE motion intelligence framework, including a new self-evolving agent capability. AGIBOT debuted GO-3 Preview, its next-generation embodied AI foundation model, showcased its WITA-Omni 1.0 omni-modal interaction model, and launched the G2 Max industrial robot and Link-U OS 1.0. The event also featured actual applications across manufacturing and commercial services, demonstrating AGIBOT’s focus on translating robotics innovation into productive work. The company said they reflect its deployment-first focus, with practical innovation spanning robot hardware, locomotion, task and interaction intelligence, operations, and an ecosystem intended to support real-world deployment at scale. Founded in 2023 as Zhiyuan Xinchuang Technology Co., AGIBOT is focused on embodied AI. The Shanghai-based company ‘s portfolio spans humanoid robots, quadrupeds , dexterous systems, and commercial cleaning systems. Last month, AGIBOT said its 20,000th robot had rolled off the production line, and IDC reported that the company led global humanoid robot shipments in the first half of 2026. Submit your innovation now! Worken is a proposed measure of robot productivity As robots move from large-scale production into increasingly diverse applications, AGIBOT said there is another dimension of progress: the productive work robots can deliver once deployed. In addition to manufacturing scale, technological capabilities, and deployment milestones, the company said sustained autonomous operation and measurable task output are increasingly important indicators of robotic value. “Over the past few years, the robotics industry has made remarkable progress in hardware, AI models, and large-scale manufacturing,” stated Peng Zhihui, co-founder, president, and chief technology officer of AGIBOT. “But as robots begin working in factories, warehouses, and service environments, we need to answer a more practical question: How much productive work are they actually delivering?” “Worken is our attempt to develop a new way of answering that question,” he added. “We want to move beyond measuring how many robots are built or delivered and begin measuring how effectively they can perform useful work, autonomously and consistently, in the real world.” Even deployments involving similar numbers of robots can deliver different levels of productivity, depending on how independently the machines operate, how frequently human intervention is required and how much acceptable work they complete. AGIBOT described Worken as “effective intelligent work hours,” bringing three factors into a proposed measurement framework: Worken = Number of Active Robots × Autonomous Working Hours × Output Efficiency Ratio The first factor counts robots actively performing tasks in real-world environments, rather than units simply manufactured or held in inventory. The second measures time spent working autonomously, rather than total powered-on time. The third factor assesses productive output against a reference benchmark for a defined task, such as the amount of acceptable work completed by a human worker under established operating standards. The Worken framework combines the number of active robots, autonomous working hours, and an output efficiency ratio to measure robot productivity in real-world deployments. Source: AGIBOT By connecting deployment scale, autonomy, and task output in Worken, AGIBOT said it wants to provide a more comprehensive way to describe robotic productivity across applications such as industrial handling, logistics, inspection, and commercial services. “The concept also opens up a broader discussion about the economics of robotics,” said the company. “While hardware depreciates over time, improvements in software and AI models may enable the same machine to perform more useful work during its operating life. Measuring that output alongside total lifecycle costs could help businesses evaluate the longer-term value of robotic deployments.” AGIBOT said Worken is an evolving framework that will be further refined through deployments and operational data. By developing task-specific benchmarks and accumulating practical experience across different applications, the company said it hopes that Worken can serve as a widely applicable reference for measuring the productive value of physical AI. The event also featured the release of the “2026 Embodied Intelligence Industry Innovation Report,” which discussed the industry’s progress toward real-world deployment. Jointly compiled by China Economic Information Service and the Shanghai Industrial Innovation Center of the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology ( CAICT ), the report included Worken and AGIBOT’s deployment examples as part of its industry analysis. AGIBOT unveils AHA3 platform and new physical AI models The AGIBOT Humanoid Architecture, or AHA3, which unifies “three intelligences in one” — locomotion, interaction, and manipulation Intelligence — in an embodied AI system. The company said it designed the third-generation hardware architecture to improve efficiency. Built on advances in motor- drive technology, integrated computing , and high-speed connectivity including Wi-Fi 6 and 5G, the AHA3 is designed to reduce integration complexity, improve system responsiveness, and support more capable robots in industrial applications. articles.title: The Most Important Thing to Remember About Your Mother
articles.snippet: “It is not easy to give closeness and freedom, safety plus danger.” One of the hardest realizations in life, and one of the most liberating, is that our mothers are neither saints nor saviors — they are just people who, however messy or painful our childhood may have been, and however complicated the adult relationship, have loved us the best way they knew how, with the cards they were dealt and the tools they had. It is a whole life’s work to accept this elemental fact, and a life’s triumph to accept it not with bitterness but with love. How to make that liberating shift of perspective is what the playwright, suffragist, and psychologist Florida Scott-Maxwell (September 14, 1883–March 6, 1979) considers in a passage from her 1968 autobiography The Measure of My Days ( public library ). Kinship by Maria Popova. (Available as a print .) She writes: A mother’s love for her children, even her inability to let them be, is because she is under a painful law that the life that passed through her must be brought to fruition. Even when she swallows it whole she is only acting like any frightened mother cat eating its young to keep it safe. In a sentiment that calls to mind Kahlil Gibran’s insight into the delicate balance of intimacy and independence essential for romantic love — which is always an echo of our formative attachments — she adds: It is not easy to give closeness and freedom, safety plus danger. Art by Alessandro Sanna from Crescendo With a wary eye to the brunt of parental expectation under which all children live, well into adulthood, she writes: No matter how old a mother is she watches her middle-aged children for signs of improvement. It could not be otherwise for she is impelled to know that the seeds of value sown in her have been winnowed. She never outgrows the burden of love, and to the end she carries the weight of hope for those she bore. Oddly, very oddly, she is forever surprised and even faintly wronged that her sons and daughters are just people, for many mothers hope and half expect that their newborn child will make the world better, will somehow be a redeemer. Perhaps they are right, and they can believe that the rare quality they glimpsed in the child is active in the burdened adult. Perhaps that glimpse is what Maurice Sendak meant when he observed that life is largely a matter of “having your child self intact and alive and something to be proud of.” Complement with Kahlil Gibran’s advice on children , the pioneering psychologist Donald Winnicott on the mother’s contribution to society , and Alison Bechdel’s superb Winnicott-inspired Are You My Mother? , then savor My Mother’s Eyes — a soulful animated short film about loss and the unbreakable bonds of love — and Mary Gaitskill’s poignant advice on how to move through life when your parents are dying . donating = loving For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a donation . Your support makes all the difference. newsletter The Marginalian has a free weekly newsletter. It comes out on Sundays and offers the week’s most inspiring reading. Here’s what to expect . Like? Sign up.
