articles.snippet: In general, LLM performance is incredibly multidimensional. There's no guarantee of a fixed ordering where the model that is best at math is also the model that's best at jokes. Despite that complexity, much of the variation in performance is explained by just a single variable: model size. In general, models that are bigger will (a) be more performant / reliable, (b) cost more per token, and (c) have better recall of esoteric facts. As you note, our models are ordered: Luna < Terra < Sol < Astra [ ... ] These days, version number signifies a few things at once: the order of release, the relationship to other releases, and the magnitude of improvement. So something like 6.1 would indicate it was launched after 5.6, may share some similarities to other 6.1 models in terms of training data / personality (which is why it's not 5.7), and isn't a giant enough leap to merit the headlines and expectations that would come with a 7. — Ted Sanders , explaining OpenAI's model naming conventions Tags: generative-ai , gpt , openai , ai , llms , ted-sanders

articles.title: Why Agents Love Supabase
articles.snippet: I first met Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson in Singapore, shortly after they finished YC as the hottest startup of YC S20 . Six years later, we finally got them on the podcast! This is their first podcast together, after taking an open-source, fully remote company from zero to a $10 billion valuation. The title is a question I wanted to understand for myself: why do agents love Supabase? There are plenty of managed databases. Postgres hosting is competitive. Being familiar to a model is useful distribution, but it doesn't explain all the work needed to turn a generated application into something that runs. But when I ran my frontier AEO tracker , it was an almost complete sweep of first choice for app backends (and in contention for managed db ) for every frontier model from Astra to Fable to Muse. At Select, Supabase grouped its announcements into Build, Operate and Scale. The things that stood out to me were surprisingly practical: start a local backend without Docker, keep the desired database schema in Git, and run compute beside the database. Each removes a piece of work that developers have been doing for years. Agents make that friction harder to ignore. Watch the full conversation, including my opening commentary → Give the agent a backend it can read My favorite developer-tool announcements make me think: of course I want this today. The new alpha runtime for running Supabase locally without Docker is one of those. I use Colima rather than Docker Desktop, and even then, removing another dependency from the path to a working database is welcome. Local setup is a small part of a human developer's week; an agent that repeatedly creates and tests environments encounters it over and over. Declarative schemas are the bigger idea. The familiar SQL workflow accumulates a history: create the schema, then migrate, migrate, migrate. A declarative representation gives the agent a description of the state you want, in files it can inspect and edit alongside the application. In the commentary, I compare this to a Terraform moment for the database. Put the desired state in Git and the agent can read it, change it, fork it and work against it as part of the repository. Humans get the same advantage: the backend becomes easier to understand without reconstructing its entire history. That is the part I like most about the agent-friendly direction. These are improvements I wanted as a developer already. Making them useful to agents gives the team another reason to finish the job. Compute deserves more than a bullet point I think Supabase Compute , now in private alpha, may be undersold. An application needs somewhere to do its work as well as somewhere to store the result. Once you have a database, you still need a place to run the processes that chunk documents, generate embeddings or do other longer-running work. Paul and Ant discuss running containers close to the database. That closes a gap between getting an application started and operating it: fewer separate services to configure, connect and explain to the agent. Edge functions remain useful, but they don't cover every workload. The operating side matters too. Logs, checks, connections and context help an agent understand what it is changing. A model that can issue SQL still needs to know what the database contains, how the application uses it, and what happened when something failed. Supabase's Operate announcements are worth reading alongside the new ways to build. From prototype to petabyte The founders say Supabase is launching about five million databases a month. They are thinking about what happens if agents push that toward billions of applications. At the same time, existing customers are growing into much larger workloads. Serving more small databases and supporting a customer's increasingly large database are different engineering problems. That helps explain the breadth of the Scale announcements : OrioleDB, Multigres and the Turso acquisition . The conversation gets into the work behind the new “prototype to petabyte” positioning, including Postgres reliability and the choices involved in scaling up and scaling out. One observation from Paul and Ant is particularly interesting for anyone building developer tools: as AI-driven usage grew, they say activation and conversion improved. Their explanation is that an agent can carry a user from signup to a working setup in one flow. The person doesn't have to figure out every configuration step before seeing the application work. We also talk about the memes and community that helped Supabase grow, open-source adoption and enterprise sales, and whether agents will converge on the same application patterns. But I wanted this episode to capture the founders' chemistry as well. It is a chance to hear Paul and Ant think through the product together—and to see how much work sits behind a backend that an agent can make look easy. Show notes Supabase Compute — run workloads alongside the database. Multigres — the team’s approach to highly available Postgres, currently in private alpha. Supabase acquires Turso — the database architecture behind its scale-out ambitions. Supabase Select — the event discussed in this conversation. Chapters 0:00 Welcome and why agents love Supabase 5:23 Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson 6:39 Compute beside the database 8:05 OrioleDB and Multigres 12:50 Scaling up, scaling out, and Turso 17:53 Developer marketing and memes 23:15 The launch and the migration 31:03 Vectors, growth, and AI recommendations 41:43 Product-led sales and enterprise growth 49:38 Live migrations and analytics 58:43 Agent-ready local development 1:06:43 Community and company workflows

articles.title: North American robot orders climb 24.8% in Q3 of 2026, says A3
articles.snippet: While automotive OEM orders declined in the first half of 2026, they picked up in Q3. Source: A3 North American companies ordered 10,989 robots valued at $723.5 million in the third quarter of 2026, according to the latest data from the Association for Advancing Automation, or A3. Orders increased 24.8% in units and 26.1% in value compared with the third quarter of 2025, making it the strongest quarter of the year so far, it said. The third-quarter gains pushed total orders for the first nine months of 2026 to 28,984 robots valued at approximately $1.89 billion, A3 reported. This represented increases of 9.6% in units and 13.3% in value over the same period last year , noted the Ann Arbor, Mich.-based organization . Orders grow in automotive in addition to other industries After declining during the first half of 2026, automotive OEM robot orders returned to positive year-over-year growth in the third quarter, increasing 7.5%, said A3. Orders from automotive component suppliers climbed 90.4%, continuing the strong demand from that segment seen earlier in the year. Several other industries recorded substantial increases in robot orders during Q3: Semiconductors and electronics /photonics: +97.6% units Plastics and rubber: +67.7% units Life sciences / pharmaceutical / biomedical : +38.7% units Metals: +37.0% units All other industries increased just 0.5% in units ordered, while food and consumer goods declined by 23.7%, A3 added. The growth in the electronics segment occurred as investment grew in U.S. semiconductor manufacturing, with strong demand for electronics supporting AI and other applications. Life sciences has also seen continued investment in domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing among others, said A3. Automotive component orders were particularly strong despite earlier weakness among automotive manufacturing, said the organization. While OEM orders improved in Q3, they remained 17% below their year-earlier level through the first nine months of 2026. “What stands out in the third quarter is not simply the magnitude of the growth, but how broadly it was distributed across the market,” stated Alex Shikany, executive vice president at A3. “Automotive OEM orders returned to positive growth, while automotive components and sectors such as semiconductors/electronics and life sciences posted significant gains. That broader mix is important because it points to a robotics market that is becoming increasingly diversified across industries and applications.” Submit your innovation now! Cobot orders increase 56%, finds A3 Force- and power-limited or collaborative robots also posted a strong third quarter, with 1,831 units valued at $63.8 million ordered. This was an increase of about 56% in units compared with Q3 2025. Collaborative robots accounted for 16.7% of all robot units ordered during the quarter. Through September, North American companies ordered 4,605 cobots valued at approximately $178 million, representing 15.9% of total robot units and 9.4% of order value. Collaborative robots continue to be used across a wide range of applications and industries. In the first nine months of 2026, cobots accounted for 43.8% of robot orders in life sciences/pharma/biomed and 36.9% in semi & electronics/photonics. Manufacturing activity continues expansion The stronger robot order numbers come alongside improving manufacturing activity, said A3. The September Institute of Supply Chain Management (ISM) Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) registered 54.5, marking a ninth consecutive month of expansion, while the Federal Reserve said that U.S. manufacturing output increasing 0.3% in September. Higher input costs, trade uncertainty, and the timing of large manufacturing projects remain factors to watch, noted A3. “But with robot orders strengthening across several industries, the North American market enters the final quarter of 2026 with positive momentum,” it said. More detailed Q3 2026 market data and graphs are available upon request for press and through the A3 Vault for member companies. A3 said it is the leading global advocate for the benefits of automating. A3 has also expanded its Market Intelligence resources with “ Business of Automation ,” a weekly show examining industry developments; Business of Automation on Substack , offering additional analysis and industry updates; and SIGNAL , a free research series covering robotics, automation, and AI. Association members seeking deeper insights can subscribe to MI+ for forecasts, detailed datasets, dashboards and industry analysis. A3 members represent more than 1,500 manufacturers, component suppliers, system integrators, end users, academic institutions, research groups, and consulting firms. The post North American robot orders climb 24.8% in Q3 of 2026, says A3 appeared first on The Robot Report .

articles.title: What Symbotic’s Walmart growth teaches robotics startups about anchor customers
articles.snippet: Symbotic’s recent quarterly filing lists its largest customer, together with affiliates, as “Customer A,” and the annual report names that customer as Walmart. Customer A supplied 90.5% of revenue in the quarter that ended June 27, 2026. Symbotic reported $720.8 million in revenue and $55 million in net income for the same quarter. Few robotics companies have turned one demanding customer into a business this size, and this profit follows earlier profits . The quarter also included $19.4 million of investment gains and negative non-GAAP free cash flow, so one quarter’s profit can’t settle whether leaning so heavily on Walmart has paid off. For a startup founder deciding whether to sign a second customer soon, Walmart’s 90.5% share says little about the cost of serving another account. I’d look at how many people that account pulls into the field and what the contract obliges each side to do when plans change. I’d also ask how easily the anchor could get the same work done another way. Walmart wrote its own insurance Symbotic can’t afford to lose Walmart, and that dependence already gives the retailer some protection. Walmart’s contracts show that it didn’t rely on that incentive alone. The 2022 master automation agreement gives Walmart continuity rights, including the right to embed engineers with Symbotic and technical material held in escrow, which Walmart can use under specified conditions. The 2025 agreement for Walmart’s store-level Accelerated Pickup and Delivery (APD) systems repeats those protections. During the APD build-out, it also caps, at a redacted number, how many comparable APD systems Symbotic can sell to each outside customer every year. The filings don’t show whether Walmart has ever tested these rights, so they read more like preparation than a proven fallback. When the APD deal closed in January 2025, Walmart committed $520 million of development funding. Symbotic paid Walmart a $200 million base price for its robotics business in the same transaction and agreed to two possible milestone payments of $175 million each. Symbotic gained funded development and the prospect of a large rollout, although the additional purchase commitment depends on performance milestones. In return, it accepted delivery obligations and limits on comparable APD sales to other customers. Every new site borrows people Operations-heavy robotics companies tend to add people as they add customers, at least until deployment becomes routine. Symbotic reported about 2,000 employees at the end of fiscal 2025, with roughly half working at customer sites to install, commission, and maintain its systems, and it brings in contractors as needed. Its standard model also has Symbotic operate a new system for a limited time before handing daily operation to the customer. Those field teams serve both new deployments and running systems, so the total can’t show what one more site would take. It does show how much of the business still happens where the robots are installed. Where the newer Symbotic demand comes from Symbotic has broadened its customer base, partly through structures it helped build. Exol, its warehouse-as-a-service venture with SoftBank, accounted for $11.6 billion of the $22.5 billion backlog at June 27, 2026, and Symbotic owns 35% of Exol and helps fund its build-out. Walmart de México, another newer customer, is majority-owned by Walmart. Exol lets customers use Symbotic’s system without buying it outright, and Walmex carries a proven relationship into a new market, so both routes make commercial sense. Both also move partly with decisions made by Symbotic or Walmart, so the longer customer list carries somewhat less independent demand than its length suggests. Submit your innovation now! A new Symbotic customer can take two years to go live Symbotic’s management said in 2023 that it aimed to add one or two new customers a year. It has also described its historical timeline as about 24 months from a signed statement of work to acceptance. Medline signed in late fiscal 2025 and plans a pilot in 2027. Associated Wholesale Grocers announced a project in March 2026 and expects operations in the fourth quarter of 2027. Associated Food Stores announced its agreement in May 2023 and had its first phase running by February 2025. Symbotic generally recognizes system revenue as it incurs costs, once acceptance is reasonably assured, so revenue can start before installation and well before go-live. The 24-month timeline instead shows how long a supplier can wait before a new customer’s site actually runs, which is when it learns whether the product traveled. What I expect and what would change my mind The scenario I would examine most closely has no villain. Walmart stays satisfied, meets its commitments, and finishes the distribution-center rollout on schedule. System revenue from that program then winds down, and the work that continues, mostly service and software, brings in less than installation did unless new system orders follow. The supplier did everything right, and its growth now depends on replacing a program that ended as planned. For Symbotic, the APD program and Exol are the obvious candidates to replace it, along with newer accounts, and I would watch whether they reach real scale before the distribution-center work tapers. I expect Walmart to remain Symbotic’s dominant customer for years, and I’d be surprised to see its share fall below 80% before fiscal 2028. Walmart keeps expanding its own commitments, with the performance-dependent APD program added on top of the distribution-center rollout. New accounts tend to start with one site or a pilot, and management’s stated aim in 2023 was one or two new customers a year. Even with revenue recognized as costs are incurred, a single new site adds little next to dozens of Walmart projects moving at once. Exol is my largest uncertainty. Its revenue counts outside Walmart, so a faster build-out of its contracted systems could pull down Walmar

articles.title: The Anthropic Prospectus Arrives: My (but not the) IPO valuation!
articles.snippet: I am a dabbler, by nature, moving on from topic to topic, but this year, I have spent more time than usual on AI, but that is because it seems to be part of almost every business or economy related story. I tried to value SpaceX ahead of and after the filing of the prospectus for its initial public offering before moving on to the question of whether it and OpenAI and Anthropic should be part of the S&P 500 index . I started my analysis of how AI would affect the rest of us , from doomsday to do-nothing scenarios, largely in response to Citrini and Citadel reports on the topic. in August 2026, I took my first big picture look at AI as a business, which I titled its bar mitzvah moment, with a look at its potential market, business economics and moats. That look was a prelude to the initial public offerings in the works (then) for Anthropic and OpenAI, and I provided a simple way to reverse engineer how much investors would need in revenues from these companies to justify their sky-high pricing. In early October, I looked at how the massive investments in AI are playing out in the aggregate earnings , cashflows and invested capital at US companies, and why it is contributing to holding the market intact, in the face of rising rates. Just last week, I argued that both Anthropic and OpenAI would be priced , rather than valued, for their initial public offerings, using what I called buzzy metrics (like annualized run rates) and promised that I would try to value the company, when it filed its prospectus. On October 26, Anthropic filed its prospectus , and at the risk of being called hopelessly wrong by both bulls and bears, I will try to value the company, using what I see as its most likely pathway, while also leaving the door open for you to disagree with me, and pick your own pathways to valuing the company. The Prospectus Before I delve into the details of the S-1 filed by Anthropic, it is worth noting that at 416 pages, it is long and filled with distractions, as has become the case with almost every initial public offering in the last two decades. (I chronicled this trend in my post on the d isclosure dilemma , arguing that while filings have become longer, they have become less informative). The Anthropic IPO has useful information that both bulls and bears will spin to justify their priors, and in the section below, I look at key disclosures, broken down by valuation input into revenue growth, profitability, risk and reinvestment categories, from both an optimist (glass half full) and pessimist (glass half empty) perspective: Revenue Growth and Composition : The good news in the revenue story is that the company has grown exponentially over the last year, with revenues in the first two quarters of this year about fourteen times as high as the revenues in the first two quarters of the last year, but the sobering news is that revenue growth slowed down in the third quarter of 2026, as OpenAI increased market share, compute capacity acted as a constraint and some enterprises moved to cheaper open source models. The good news on customer composition is that the number of enterprises that spend more than $1 million a year on Claude increased to 1900 , from less than a hundred a year ago, but the bad news is that the company still has concentrated revenues , with its top five customers accounting for 25% of revenues. Operating and Net Profitability : In bad news, Anthropic reported an operating loss, corrected for non-cash and one-time charges, of over $ 8 billion, for the first six months of the year. The actual loss reported was $80 billion, but $72 billion represented a non-cash charge, expensing the conversion option of the convertible bond. The good news, though, is that not only are the trend lines working in their favor, with the company claiming that it had an operating profit in the most recent quarter. The company is also delivering its revenues more efficiently over time, with all of its expenses decreasing as a percent of revenues across the quarters, with compute costs, its biggest cost,, decreasing from more than 250% of revenues to 48% of revenues, on a quarterly basis. Reinvestment for growth : AI agents are computing power hogs, and AI companies invest immense amounts in compute power. The financial statements in Anthropic's prospectus actually do not show this investment at the moment, with neither the cap ex in the statement of cash flow nor the debt (and invested capital) in the balance sheet showing substantial investment in compute power. Before you accuse Anthropic of hiding the truth (or worse), the company is open about its future compute power commitments, reporting hundreds of billions in compute commitments in future years. The good news is that Anthropic is now catching up with OpenAI, which had the lead on compute power, but the bad news is that this catching up has not been cheap, in terms of cost commitments in future years. It i s also worth noting that compute power will need to be renewed and reinvested in, and while chip costs (a key component) may come down, data centers, facing opposition from communities, may become more expensive. Operating and Regulatory risk : Anthropic's argument is that its customers, once they adopt Claude models within their enterprises, will find that they become so integral to operations that they will not abandon them (making revenues sticky and the business less risky). That has not been fully tested yet, and it is entirely possible that spending on AI agents is cyclical and that companies will pull back in bad times. On the financing front, committing to hundreds of billons in compute, purchase and lease commitments exposes the firm to default risk (with a bond rating of BB+), but in response the company will argue that its access to new capital, as a publicly traded large market-cap company, will make this risk recede. In addition, its cash balance, already at $114 billion, and likely to be bulked up with another $100 bill

articles.title: GitHub Octoverse 2026
articles.snippet: GitHub Octoverse 2026 I'm at GitHub Universe today (GitHub gave me a free ticket through their "GitHub Stars" program). EVP Jay Parikh just announced this year's Octoverse report, and highlighted these numbers in particular: This is a pretty stark representation of the impact of agentic engineering on GitHub. In 2026, merged pull requests tripled in less than a year to 220 million per month. Commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month, with most of that increase in the second half of this year. New repository rate doubled this year, to 30.3 million per month. The report includes new numbers by industry, and breaks out numbers for repositories that involve "interoperability or reverse engineering". The methodology section includes notes about how they did this: Top countries by pushes to public repositories, adjusted by profile location . Pushes from each country were summed across the Octoverse year. To adjust for biases caused by VPN usage, LLM classification was used to extract the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code from the profiles of GitHub users who contributed pushes during this period [...] Industry . Public repositories created 2022 to 2026 were sorted into NAICS sectors by a fine-tuned multilingual embedding model using name, description, topics, and README, from random samples per year. [...] Interoperability . Counts public repositories created each year whose name, description, topics, or README mention interoperability or reverse engineering, or related terms, such as clean room implementation, drop-in replacement, or protocol re-implementation. articles.title: Warp Sciences emerges from stealth, to apply robotics to drug research
articles.snippet: Warp Sciences plans to create chemistry infrastructure for sovereign biotech. Source: deni AI, Adobe Stock Warp Sciences last week emerged from stealth with $215 million in funding to create infrastructure that enables biotech and pharmaceutical companies to discover new medicines faster. The startup said it is building a U.S.-based chemistry contract research organization, or CRO, to bring together chemists, robotics, and AI to make and test molecules for research teams. The South San Francisco-based company ‘s stated goal is to provide experimental data to train better AI that in turn enables more capable labs, giving scientists the ability to test more ideas. “AI has dramatically accelerated software engineering and mathematics, but it has yet to make the same impact in the physical sciences,” stated Kevin Weil , co-founder and CEO of Warp Sciences. “Chemistry and biology move forward when you make something, test it and learn from the result.” “If we want to build more capable AI for science, we need to generate real-world data at scale,” he added. “Warp is starting that process by making the research compounds drug discovery needs today, while building the labs and automation to speed the cycle from hypothesis to experiment to answer.” Warp said it has no proprietary drug pipeline itself; it is designing automated labs that can run experiments, learn from them, and improve with each cycle. Warp Sciences focuses on sovereign biotechnology A promising molecular design is only the beginning, observed Warp Sciences. “Scientists have to make it, test it, and use what they learn to decide what comes next,” said the company. “Faster access to compounds gives research teams faster answers, more ideas to pursue, and more opportunities to find medicines that change lives.” Warp also noted the importance of sovereign biotechnology. In a 2024 survey by the Biotechnology Innovation Organization, 74% reported contracts with Chinese companies for preclinical and clinical services, according to Reuters. The BIOSECURE Act , signed into law in December 2025, established a framework for restrictions on federal procurement and funding involving designated biotechnology companies of concern. In response, Warp claimed that it is building a U.S.-based chemistry partner that scientists can rely on for its speed, quality, and close collaboration. Its goal is to shorten the path from molecular design to testing while giving customers more control over where sensitive research takes place. The company said its initial service will focus on lead optimization analog synthesis, making variations of molecules that scientists can compare as they search for a drug candidate. Experienced chemists will guide experiments as the lab is increasingly automated by robotics and AI, with AI models trained on data from physical experiments. Warp plans to enable its customers to discover drugs more efficiently and keep that discovery in the U.S. Submit your innovation now! Founders’ expertise spans AI and healthcare Warp Sciences noted that its founding team ’s experience spans AI, data infrastructure, healthcare, and drug discovery. Weil most recently served as chief product officer and vice president of science at OpenAI . Chief Scientific Officer Solomon “Sol” Reisberg held medicinal chemistry leadership roles at Terremoto Biosciences. “I’ve worked with overseas chemistry partners that delivered speed and value, but I still worried about protecting the intellectual property behind our programs,” said Reisberg. “We’re building Warp to give drug hunters that same caliber of chemistry services in the U.S., with IP protection at the center of the relationship, and without the price premium that U.S. boutique CROs currently demand.” Chief Technology Officer “ Manohar “Mano” Paluri was a vice president at Meta Superintelligence Labs and a founding member of FAIR. DJ Patil was a founding executive at Devoted Health and the first U.S. chief data scientist for the White House. “Our goal is simple: Every experiment should make the next one smarter,” Paluri asserted. “AI needs a closer connection to the physical work of chemistry. Closing the loop between designing experiments, executing them, and learning from their outcomes builds increasingly capable systems for deciding what to make and how to make it. We’re building the software, AI and robotics alongside the lab so each part is shaped by what chemists actually need.” Early hires have added robotics experience from companies including Genesis , Skild AI , and 1X Technologies , as well as scientific expertise from Genentech and Lawrence Livermore National Labs. “Warp’s services bolster customer-led discovery programs. Our biotech and pharma customers determine which molecules to pursue and retain control of their drug programs,” said Patil. “We’re not developing drugs of our own. We’re building the infrastructure for the people who do.” Venture capital firms, angel investors support Warp Lightspeed led Warp Sciences’ funding, with participation from Premji Invest, Mayfield, IVP, Lux, Conviction, Menlo Ventures, 01 Advisors, Standard, Lowercarbon Capital, Gigascale Capital, Angular Ventures, Scribble Ventures, Uncork Capital, Innovation Endeavors, Matter VP, Zero Shot Fund, SignalFire and Moxxie Ventures. Angel investors included Brian Armstrong (Coinbase CEO), Mike Krieger (Anthropic Labs co-lead, Instagram co-founder), Milan Kovac (former Tesla Robotics vice president), and Ion Stoica (Databricks co-founder). It also included Fidji Simo (former OpenAI AGI Deployment CEO), Brendan Foody (Mercor CEO), Mark Chen (OpenAI chief research officer), and Sarah Friar (OpenAI chief financial officer). In addition, Kate Rouch (former OpenAI and Coinbase chief marketing officer), Lulu Meservey (Rostra CEO), Deepak Pathak (Skild AI CEO), Dylan Field (Figma CEO), and Lachy Groom ( Physical Intelligence co-founder and chief operating officer) were angel investors. The post Warp Sciences emerges

articles.snippet: NVIDIA RTX Spark powers thin and light laptops built for everything that developers, creators and gamers do. RTX Spark laptops are now available from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI. These powerful systems combine an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU and an NVIDIA Grace CPU in a single superchip with up to 128GB of unified memory and up to 1 petaflop of FP4 AI performance. That puts the NVIDIA CUDA platform, RTX graphics and the capabilities of a personal AI supercomputer inside premium Windows laptops built to go anywhere. New and expected RTX Spark updates, coming soon, include: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, an open weight speech model for transcription, speaker attribution and translation is available on RTX Spark. The LFM3 family of open models with day-zero support. Resource management controls in NVIDIA App to allocate GPU resources between foreground apps and background agents. Phantom Blade Zero , S-GAME’s highly-anticipated action role-playing game, launches with ray tracing and NVIDIA DLSS 4.5. Experience Minecraft with path tracing and DLSS with RTX Remix1.6, available now for RTX Spark. Turn Recorded Audio Into Useful Information With NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe Introduced today, NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe is a new, open weight speech model that turns recorded conversations into useful information. Instead of needing multiple models for transcription, speaker labels and translation, developers can use one promptable model that handles all three, plus questions about the audio. It transcribes 40 languages, including seven Indic languages. Developers guide the model with plain-language prompts. For example, for a single recorded meeting, users can ask it to: “Transcribe this recording and label each speaker.” “Translate this audio into English.” “List what decisions were made in this meeting.” Prompts can also include product terms and formatting conventions, which helps the model handle specialized vocabulary in fields like healthcare, financial services and customer service. Because the weights are open, developers can choose where audio is processed, from a desktop to the cloud. Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe ranks No. 1 on the Hugging Face Open ASR and No. 2 among open weight models on Artificial Analysis — delivering leading accuracy with approximately 4.3 billion active parameters, 80% fewer than the No. 1 open weight model, making high-quality, intelligent transcription more practical on local hardware. It’s available today on Hugging Face . Quantized versions are coming soon, so developers can run Transcribe locally onNVIDIA RTX Spark and DGX Spark systems, Jetson AGX Thor devices or scale up on NVIDIA Blackwell data center GPUs. NVFP4 versions will be deployable through NeMo-Speech.cpp or vLLM. Learn more in the NVIDIA technical blog . Control How Agents and PC Apps Share GPU Resources On RTX Spark, users can have long-running agents working alongside their favorite applications. Both share the system’s GPU compute, and the right balance of resources depends on what matters to users at that moment. With the new resource management feature in NVIDIA App , users can now choose how GPU resources are shared. They can prioritize their foreground app for the best performance, or give their background-running agent more resources to get work done faster. Access control resource sharing from System > Advanced in the NVIDIA App. This feature requires hardware-accelerated GPU scheduling to be enabled in Windows Settings. Liquid AI : One Model Family, Many Ways to Work Liquid AI’s LFM3 provides a new generation of Liquid Foundation Models designed for specialized tasks. The family spans text, vision, audio, omni and decision models built on one shared backbone, with base and post-trained models available as open weights. The models are compact and fast: Liquid AI’s new 1.7-billion-parameter base model outperforms its previous 2.6-billion-parameter base model. These models support local workflows such as agents running in Hermes Agent, Pi and OpenClaw to triage inboxes and manage calendars, read documents and app screens, transcribe and translate speech, answer spoken questions about handwritten math, and route support tickets or voice requests. Developers can run LFM3 models on RTX Spark with native support through llama.cpp and vLLM, and fine-tune the models locally. ‘Phantom Blade Zero’ Launches With DLSS 4.5 S-GAME’s Phantom Blade Zero launches tonight, Oct. 28, at 7 p.m. PT on Steam and the Epic Games Store . Players can take on the role of Soul, a swordsman framed for his master’s murder, as he travels the martial world to uncover a conspiracy. NVIDIA worked with S-GAME Studio and S-GAME Publishing to add ray-traced effects to the title. On RTX Spark laptops and GeForce RTX GPU-powered PCs, ray tracing adds more accurate bounced lighting, detailed reflections and realistic shadows on foliage and terrain. The NVIDIA DLSS Dynamic Multi Frame Generation feature boosts frame rates with up to 6x frame generation, or adjusts the multiplier on the fly to hit a player’s target frame rate. Read more on GeForce.com . RTX Remix Breathes New Life Into Classics NVIDIA RTX Remix , the modding platform for remastering classic games with path tracing and DLSS, released version 1.6 last week. This update brought RTX Remix to the world’s largest gaming community: Minecraft . Both creators and players can render Minecraft Java Edition 1.21.1 through RTX Remix with DLSS-accelerated path tracing and take full advantage of realistic lighting and materials in their future creations. The update also adds DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering, up to 6x Multi Frame Generation, native RTX Spark support and agent-assisted workflows. Starting today, those upgrades come to Portal with RTX and the Half-Life 2 RTX demo. Both now support RTX Spark, with DLSS 3D-Guided Neural Rendering for more lifelike lighting and materials, a new Performance Mode for DLSS Frame Generation and new options that speed up

articles.title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe and Granary v2: Intelligent Multilingual Transcription You Can Prompt and Adapt
The October inflection point for vibe game development
articles.snippet: I've written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents - the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we've reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it's for vibe coding computer games . Tree Appreciator Emberwick Battle Drones Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove Four times as insulting What happens if someone actually puts the work in? You should build a game! Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game: 3D modeling Music generation (see Scrimshaw Jukebox ) Game design (!) That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments . The challenge has been getting to a game that's actually fun to play . Game design is a deep subject area. I won't pretend to be well versed in it - I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn't think the models could do it. Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to "Make it a LOT more fun"... and it did . In the past few weeks I've vibe coded (in the classic sense of the term - no looking at the code at all) four games that I've genuinely enjoyed playing. I attended Foo Camp in Berkeley over the weekend and met several people who were having similar experiences. Building games that play well is shockingly easy now. The new challenge is coming up with concepts for games that are novel and delightful and that wouldn't exist without AI assistance. I haven't done an exhaustive study, but my current impression is that GPT-6 Astra isn't quite there yet. It can absolutely build a game, but its sense of fun doesn't match that of Opus 5.5. I expect OpenAI will get there by the end of the year. Here are the four game projects that have convinced me that the models are now capable of producing fun games with very little guidance. All four are built in HTML and JavaScript and run entirely in the browser. Tree Appreciator The smallest game I found to be genuinely delightful is Tree Appreciator . I used the regular Claude chat interface for this - it didn't even need Claude Code. I built this on a whim while we were driving along Skyline Boulevard looking at trees. My prompt was: Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful. I've found that telling models to use three.js works really well. Claude doesn't have its own image generation model but is capable of building full-color 3D models that look and feel excellent. This game required no iteration or follow-up prompting at all - I got the game in a single shot. It gave me back a charming little mobile-friendly spot-the-difference game. You can play that here . Here's the chat transcript that built it. It's pleasingly relaxing. The graphics are fun, and collecting trees that you have completed in a "herbarium" provides a nice, cosy sense of accomplishment. Emberwick This was a more ambitious project that I again built using regular Claude chat. I started out by building an experimental prototype of an engine for a top-down fantasy RPG: Build a demo game engine three.js which is a top down (but at an angle) RPG - the player gets to move through the world with one or two companions. Create a fantasy village setting that demonstrates walking around outside and then shows how when the player enters a building the wall between the player and the camera goes transparent so the user can see what is happening Add some NPCs and plenty of furniture and different types of building some with an upstairs - be creative, make it look great Here's that first version . It worked really well! I was inspired to increase my ambitions: Make it not so flat - the buildings are great but the landscape itself is completely flat at the moment, fix that Add basements to two of the buildings with a tunnel system joining them below the village Add the start of a rocky mountain on one side of the village containing a cave with a sleeping troll Here's that version . When that produced a good result, I decided to push it all the way: Now turn this into an actual game - quadruple the size of the playable area, introduce fun game mechanics, add a plot that isn't too cliche, some twists, a magic system, make it really good We're back to prompts like "make it really good" here! Asking for a plot that "isn't too cliche" seemed to work too - it's a bit cliché, but still novel enough that I enjoyed following the story. Unlike Tree Appreciator, this took quite a bit of additional playtesting and prompting to get to a finished version. This was mainly due to gameplay problems - things like a character not being in the right place to complete a quest because a different story element had caused them to move to another location. Here's that final game . It has a full story that takes about 15 minutes to play through. There's even an experimental level editor if you want to drop in your own houses, furniture, and landscape features. Once it was all working (and I'd iterated through some gameplay bugs), I played it through from start to finish and found myself emotionally affected by the ending! I'm somewhat embarrassed by this, because everything in this game - the graphics, the plot, the characters, the music, the dialog - came from the model. My creative input was pretty much just "it's a fantasy village and there's a troll asleep in a cave". Here's the full shared Claude chat in which I built this game. I also fed that same initial sequence of prompts through ChatGPT GPT-6 Pro. Here

articles.title: WorldOracle Tests Whether World Models Can Reliably Predict Real-World Executions
articles.snippet: Key Takeaways WorldOracle is a benchmark for action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) that scores each model’s predicted rollout against the paired real-world execution, with both starting from the same initial observations and following the same action sequence. Seven representative models were evaluated; arm motion was predicted relatively well, but object positions and movements often deviated from reality, and performance dropped over complete operation sequences. The platform opened to developers on October 16 and accepts both open-weight and closed-source models. In one WorldOracle case, the robot’s grasp missed, yet the world model predicted a successful pick. Credit: [WorldOracle team / AgiBot] In one case showcased by WorldOracle, a robot’s grasp missed, yet the world model predicted that the robot had successfully picked up the fruit. Given the initial frame and action sequence of a real manipulation episode, the model generated a rollout that looked plausible on screen but differed from the actual execution. The success it depicted never happened in reality. Researchers from Princeton University, the University of Texas at Austin, the University of Toronto, NVIDIA and AgiBot have jointly introduced WorldOracle, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) by comparing their predictions with real-world executions that start from the same initial observations and follow the same action sequences. The team evaluated seven representative models — among them DreamDojo, Cosmos 3, IRASim and GE-Sim 2.0 — and identified two prominent problems. First, while the motion paths of robot arms are predicted relatively well, the positions and movements of manipulated objects can still deviate from reality. Second, models that perform well over short horizons can degrade significantly over complete operation sequences. On October 16, WorldOracle, an evaluation platform for action-conditioned world models, officially opened to developers. The research team has collected real manipulation episodes in advance, recording both video and actions. Developers use the initial frames and action sequences provided in the evaluation set to generate predicted videos and submit them to the platform, which scores each submission against the corresponding real execution record. The results show whether a model has accurately predicted the consequences of the actions, helping developers pinpoint weaknesses and verify improvements. Project page: https://worldoracle-benchmark.github.io/ Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18826 How Do Seven World Models Perform? Arm motion is right, but objects don’t always follow The predicted motion of a robot arm reaching toward a piece of fruit and closing its gripper may closely match its actual motion, yet the model can still incorrectly predict whether the fruit is lifted and where it moves next. To assess the two separately, the research team compared the position and motion of the robot arm and of the manipulated object in each predicted video against the real-world recording, and scored them individually. Spatial alignment scores for the robot arm and the manipulated object. Credit: [WorldOracle team / AgiBot] The results show that all five models evaluated on the human-operated AgiBot G2 data scored higher on the arm than on the object. In other words, even when the arm in the generated video follows the given actions well, the position and movement of the object may still depart from reality. IRASim scored 78.8 on the robot arm but only 29.1 on the manipulated object, while Cosmos 3 scored 89.4 and 45.4, respectively. The remaining models showed gaps of varying size. Accuracy declines as the rollout horizon grows Time presents a second challenge. Completing a continuous task often requires multiple grasps, placements and adjustments, and the object state left by one interaction becomes the starting point for the next. Whether a model stays close to reality must therefore be tested over the full process. WorldOracle evaluates both the first 30 seconds of each trajectory and the complete long sequence. WorldOracle-SV scores of the same models under the two evaluation horizons. Credit: [WorldOracle team / AgiBot] On the same set of AgiBot G2 teleoperation data, the WorldOracle-SV scores of all five models fell. DreamDojo dropped from 50.56 to 27.08, and Cosmos 3 from 53.99 to 26.60, nearly halving in both cases. GE-Sim 2.0 fell from 73.86 to 63.33; it posted the highest score of the five models at both horizons and the smallest decline over the full sequence. The relative ranking also shifted. IRASim scored below Ctrl-World, DreamDojo and Cosmos 3 over the first 30 seconds, but above all three over the full sequence. What Can WorldOracle Measure? WorldOracle evaluation framework: real actions are recorded, the model predicts what follows, and the result is scored against the real execution. Credit: [WorldOracle team / AgiBot] Accurately predicting a failure earns a high score WorldOracle starts from pre-collected records of real manipulation. A model is given the initial frame and the action sequence and generates a predicted video, which is compared with the real execution of the same actions. What models must predict includes missed grasps, drops and spills. If an operation fails in reality, accurately predicting that failure counts as a correct prediction. Failed executions therefore serve as an important class of test samples: they reveal whether a model follows the given actions and their consequences, or defaults to a successful version of the task. The benchmark covers two robot embodiments, AgiBot G2 and YAM, as well as first-person human-hand manipulation. Four tasks (fruit picking, towel hanging, water pouring and drawer pulling) involve interaction with rigid, deformable, fluid and articulated objects, respectively. Task coverage varies by embodiment, as defined in the evaluation set. The human-hand setting is intended fo

articles.title: Artificial Analysis v5 and the benchmarker's dilemma
articles.snippet: Hill-climbing is easy, knowing what to hill-climb is hard. Making scores go up is expensive , but we have a much clearer playbook for it than we do for creating meaningful benchmarks at the true frontier of AI today. Independent evaluation of language models is under-appreciated in how hard of a task it is. These groups are not just taking current models and certifying their scores, which is a technically involved task. This is their job if AI progress is slow. When AI progress is as fast as it is, the technical details of the job are the routine work part of trying to put a single number on what makes for a good AI model today. The goal is to have a single number that is representative of current models, matching vibe checks, community sentiment, and scientific analysis, while being forward looking enough so that it’s not outdated in 3 months. Everyone building a benchmark faces a sort of paradox. You need your benchmark to reduce to one single number, so that it is easy to discuss, use in reports, and compare models, but every method of aggregating scores comes with meaningful trade-offs. The best scientists need to do this, everyone does. It’s a matter of creating aggregation metrics that you think are most fair, knowing there will always be imperfections. With the amount of money in the AI ecosystem today, the weight of independent evaluation is even higher – you dictate the winners and losers of a trillion dollar market. You also influence some of the models themselves, steering the shape of progress. This is a lot of pressure! My prompt for this article is Artificial Analysis’s recent update to their Intelligence Index, v5 . The AA index is the most prominent independent intelligence metric for the latest frontier models, followed in a distant second by Epoch AI’s Capabilities Index (ECI) . To date, all of these have been incredibly useful for the community and massively flawed! Interconnects AI is a reader-supported publication. Consider becoming a subscriber. Language models are capable of so much today, and this scope of capabilities is growing quickly. Our era of singular intelligence indices should be phased out soon, but it will take a long time. A summary of AAv5 is below, from their blog post, where they describe it as “reflecting real-world usage today:” Intelligence Index v5 weights: ➤ Knowledge Work (25%): AA-Briefcase (15%), AutomationBench-AA (5%), and GDP.pdf (5%) ➤ Coding (25%): FrontierCode 2.0 (15%) and Terminal-Bench 4.0 (10%) ➤ Science (25%): Terminal-Bench-Science (15%) and CritPt v2 hard subset (10%) ➤ General (25%): AA-Omniscience v1.1 15% (10% accuracy, 5% non-hallucination) and HLE-Diamond (10%) Here’s the new ranking of models: The problem with trying to benchmark real-world usage today is that it is extremely jagged, just like the models. The most proven use-case is coding, where open models are far more competitive and likely to keep up. In knowledge work, I’m less confident in open models. At first glance, in aggregate, their model ranking definitely looks reasonable. Still, it shows signs of strain and confusion, as any benchmark will, with GPT 6.1 Terra beating Claude Fable 5.1 on AAv5. Today, some benchmarks measure the absolute frontier of capabilities, playing nicely in open-ended tasks through your favorite harness, which often does take a large model. Some other benchmarks measure certain skills that will be needed of a model in repetitive agentic tasks. I get the feeling that AA is tuning their benchmark more towards the former, a general agentic collaborator, but all of these behaviors overlap. This takes us to the plot going around that prompted me to write this, where they showed the balance of open vs. closed models on the new benchmark. This plot shows 8 closed models beating the best to-be open-weight model, Kimi K3.1 Pro (which isn’t colored blue). This benchmark is taking the opinion of trying to measure where frontier models are moving into, which grows the gap to open models. This is an okay decision to take, but over time as existing workflows of open models become key factors of the economy, it could become a benchmark that misses where the core economic engine of the industry is. Open models’ demise from this seems greatly exaggerated, but I do think the previous index was flattering the open weight models too strongly. Consider this plot from the Kimi K3.1 Pro launch — yes, the open models are strong and useful in some cases, but the best OpenAI and Anthropic models have been a major step ahead in their flexibility and reliability. Some of the evaluations in AAv5 that open models are most behind on are “science” evals like terminal-bench-science and CritPT v2 . Open models are behind, but the value proposition was never to compete truly at the frontier. The open model economy will be about Reducing domains with high market demand for inference to a commodity price of hardware. Allowing ownership of intelligence, specializing it to internal data, and controlling internal agents across many companies in the economy. Both of these will take a very long time to materialize and are partially represented in benchmarks. The supply of compute is currently so low that open model providers also are raking in solid margins – when this shrinks, we will know the system is starting to work. The same goes for diffusion into enterprises, it’s not clear what the exact ceiling on it is because of the difficult ML expertise that is needed to build evaluations and do post-training today. Share At the next major model cycle, say in 2-3 months with GLM 6 or Kimi 3.5, I expect the leading open model labs to make substantial steps on this index, again surprising many observers. This is a cycle we have been on for years now. I’ve written many times about how open models keep up with the frontier, and a summary is that: The best open models do benchmax a little. The worst open models benchmax a lot (but don’t get a ton of attention anyways). The best open mo

articles.snippet: My mid-week morning reads: • I went to Mexico to test-drive the cars Americans can’t buy : Mexico is a showroom for electric cars, with a growing fleet of sleek new vehicles from Chinese brands unavailable to Americans. ( Washington Post free ) • Homeownership Helped Make America. It’s Slipping Away for Millions . ( Barron’s ) see also The Superrich Are Buying $100 Million Mansions Just to Tear Them Down : In March 2023 William Lauder paid $155 million for Rush Limbaugh’s Palm Beach estate, a 24,000-square-foot house with a Versailles-style salon and a Biltmore-style library. Now they fear a reckoning . Police kept access to Flock’s vast surveillance system long after they left the force. Some used it to track the locations of romantic partners. ​( Washington Post ) • Neutrinos Are Everywhere. articles.title: [AINews] Anthropic ends Coding Interviews: "Hunger beats tenure"
articles.snippet: Several midsize headlines today; on top of some impressive Math verification , Google Genie and Artificial Analysis and FrontierCode all shipped major version bumps of their top offerings, all of which have been AINews title stories in the past, but are mostly annual incremental improvements. Past guest Felix Reiseberg gets the headline today for coming out and charting the path forward for junior engineers : “ Hunger beats tenure” This month, I laid the traditional coding interview to rest. As a hiring manager at Anthropic, I stopped asking candidates to do them… …There’s no more point in giving you a little React challenge than there is in quizzing people about assembly; Claude is now better at both. Our most impactful builders are successful regardless of how good they are at these tests. Enough said. His advice for juniors Pick business impact over backlog : In pre-AI-coding 2011, Patrick McKenzie wrote “engineers are hired to create business value, not to program things.” Pick a radical idea : Come up with a few ideas that would, if successful, dramatically improve the chances that your organization achieves those goals. Be ambitious! Build it over a weekend : I have seen small groups and solo engineers fly past the usual process of writing product requirements documents (PRDs), getting buy-in, and lobbying for time with designers or product managers by building a working prototype. Focus on one good idea : In my experience, junior people often make the mistake of cramming multiple ideas into a single prototype , hiding three excellent ideas among 20 bad ones. Lean into your fresh perspective : If you’re working on something user-facing, you have a unique amount of empathy for users and thus a much better sense for how the product works or doesn’t work for them. Well said, Felix! Get web search results as clean, structured Markdown, using roughly 50% fewer tokens than JSON on average. Easily integrate Markdown search results into your AI workflows across 100+ SerpApi APIs! swyx’s commentary: we’re proud to work with AI native sponsors that you can use in your engineering workflows! Check out the token savings of Markdown - from 361k tokens to 38k for Google properties! AI Twitter Recap Genie 4: DeepMind's Real-Time World Model Adds Audio, Physics and Gemini Planning Launch : Google DeepMind introduced Genie 4, its "most realistic and interactive world model yet." Users can explore generated environments in real time and steer events, camera angles and actions with text ( GDM , Sundar Pichai , Demis Hassabis ). Architecture : The model is built on Gemini Omni. Gemini runs in the loop to plan multi-step events and keep scenes coherent ( features , Eli Collins ). Native audio : It generates ambient sound, music and real-time dialogue with characters, a first for Genie ( Shlomi Fruchter ). Physics and photorealism : DeepMind claims aerodynamics, collisions and natural human motion. Genie 3's worlds were "too static," and Genie 4 responds to prompted events mid-generation ( Fruchter ). Robotics angle : DeepMind positions Genie 4 as a step toward safe virtual environments for testing agents and robots. Demos : Gemini 3.8 Flash decomposes tasks, checks each step and replans as the scene changes. A Gemini 4 Argon + Genie 4 experiment simulates an Apollo humanoid playing checkers ( summary ). Availability : The research preview is open to trusted testers now. Google AI Ultra subscribers will get access next via Project Genie, followed by early-access partners through the Gemini API and AI Studio, which marks Genie's first API availability ( Logan Kilpatrick , waitlist ). Early-access impressions : Users with early access describe prompting a "neogothic brutalist city," then adding dragons and an NPC live. They call it "not flawless" but a large leap over Genie 3 ( Ethan Mollick , venturetwins , Riley Goodside ). AI for Math and Science: CFSG Formalized, ETH Disproof Claims Axiom formalizes CFSG : Axiom announced a complete Lean auto-formalization of the Classification of Finite Simple Groups. The original proof spans about 15,000 pages across roughly 500 papers by more than 100 mathematicians ( Axiom , Kevin Weil ). Process : An agent swarm produced about 50M lines of Lean in 24 days. Agents claimed tasks, reviewed each other's work and merged through GitHub, with human guidance, and reportedly fixed hundreds of errata in the published proof ( omarsar0 , kimmonismus ). Context : Researchers note it displaces the four-color theorem as the largest computer-verified proof. Few humans understand the full CFSG proof ( hyhieu226 , Stella Biderman ). Exponential Time Hypothesis : OpenAI announced new results in harmonic analysis, complexity theory and QFT, including a claimed refutation of ETH, with materials in its openai/math repo ( Romain Huet , Dan ). Anthropic's parallel claim : Anthropic reportedly says Claude independently disproved ETH, finding the key algorithm on Oct 16 with "14M output tokens and no human input." PSI also claims progress on five open quantum physics problems with computer-checked proofs ( Rundown roundup ). Physics follow-up : A Yang-Mills Working Group published a statement interpreting an AI result related to the existence of quantum Yang-Mills theory ( KITP ). Smaller results : Ten Claude agents proved in Lean that seven electrons on a sphere settle into a pentagonal bipyramid, a case of the Thomson problem ( Vals ). Separately, a Stanford study had 29 experts rate AI-proposed research problems and judged about one-third "interesting" ( Percy Liang ). Independent Evals: AA Index v5, FrontierCode 2.0 and GPT-6.1 Terra Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 : 60% of the index now comes from private or held-out sets ( announcement ). Composition : It adds FrontierCode 2.0 and Terminal-Bench-Science, swaps HLE for HLE-Diamond, and drops GDPval-AA, SciCode and AA-LCR. Four categories carry equal 25% weights ( weights ). articles.title: What It Takes to Be Free
articles.snippet: We spend our lives trying to find our power and our freedom. It is not easy: We live in a culture that has distorted the meaning and measure of power, confusing visibility with value, status with substance, attention with love; we live in a universe where free will may be an illusion , where chance deals the vast majority of the cards — the family and epoch we are born into, the body and biochemistry we live in, the people we cross paths with, the accidents of chemistry and happenstance we call love. The great double-edged question is how to keep power from becoming a prison and how much freedom we can find between the narrow parameters of our givens. But somewhere deep down, in the marrow of our language, we seem to know: The word power shares its Middle Latin root with possibility — its only measure is that which liberates the possible in us; our only power is our freedom. Art from An Almanac of Birds: 100 Divinations for Uncertain Days , also available as a stand-alone print and as stationery cards . “Nothing is more unbearable, once one has it, than freedom,” James Baldwin wrote . It is unbearable largely because it demands a shedding of the self with all of its attachments — to ways of being, to ideas about how the world ought to be, to particular interpretations of reality. Such attachments are shackles best broken by what Irish Murdoch has so splendidly termed unselfing , key to each of the five kinds of freedom she identified in literature and life. For Murdoch, freedom takes radical unsefling — only then are we truly free to both be ourselves and love each other: Freedom is exercised in the confrontation by each other, in the context of an infinitely extensible work of imaginative understanding, of two irreducibly dissimilar individuals. Love is the imaginative recognition of, that is respect for, this otherness. This is why, for Octavio Paz — who thought deeply about freedom — love is “a knot made of two intertwined freedoms.” And if love is our fulcrum of belonging, then belonging itself is woven of the same paradox — something Maya Angelou articulates in one of her finest interviews : You only are free when you realize you belong no place — you belong every place — no place at all. Art by Ofra Amit for The Dark Wood of the Golden Birds by Margaret Wise Brown In this sense, freedom is the hinge between being and belonging that swings open the door to being ourselves — which, yet again paradoxically, must include the freedom to change, to confront the illusory solidity of the self, its ceaseless mutability. Psychoanalyst Karen Horney formulates this perfectly in her pioneering work on the fundaments of personal growth : We do not need an inner strait jacket with which to shackle our spontaneity, nor the whip of inner dictates to drive us to perfection. There is no doubt that such disciplinary methods can succeed in suppressing undesirable factors, but there is also no doubt that they are injurious to our growth. We do not need them because we see a better possibility of dealing with destructive forces in ourselves: that of actually outgrowing them. The way toward this goal is an ever increasing awareness and understanding of ourselves. Self-knowledge, then, is not an aim in itself, but a means of liberating the forces of spontaneous growth… And as we lose the neurotic obsession with self, as we become free to grow ourselves, we also free ourselves to love and to feel concern for other people. Then, and only then, can we contact the soul beneath the self , which is the only real locus of our freedom. Vassily Grossman — who spent a thousand days as a correspondent on the frontlines of the Holocaust — captures this beautifully in a passage from his almost unbearably poignant reckoning with life and death : What constitutes the freedom, the soul of an individual life, is its uniqueness. The reflection of the universe in someone’s consciousness is the foundation of his or her power, but life only becomes happiness, is only endowed with freedom and meaning when someone exists as a whole world that has never been repeated in all eternity. Only then can they experience the joy of freedom and kindness, finding in others what they have already found in themselves. donating = loving For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). articles.title: How Anthropic ships Claude with Claude: Separating the Brain from the Hands
articles.snippet: Watch the full episode on YouTube As we learned from the Anthropic S-1 filings yesterday , the lab has some of the highest revenue and research efficiency in human history, particularly with -126% loss to 19% GAAP profit turnaround in the last year. The company credits this to their two core loops: Improvement and Investment: Today we go inside how Anthropic works. Now the dust has settled on Opus 5.5 and it has lasted a month as the generally accepted #1 LLM in the world, we dive into its launch, and how Anthropic ships Claude with Claude with Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang , heads of Engineering and Product respectively. The team is working under two kinds of pressure. The models are getting more capable, which makes safe deployment and access decisions harder. At the same time, usage is growing fast enough that ordinary infrastructure choices—like how much CPU an API consumes—become strategic. Those problems meet in the product choices that reach developers. A model launch is also an API launch Anthropic's Opus 5.5 launch emphasizes both model quality and cost. We discuss feedback that the previous Opus generations were be too verbose, alongside the need for stronger intelligence per dollar. Anthropic says the new model costs less to run than its predecessor; the exact saving depends on the workload and its use of cached context. The less visible launch work involves changes to how people integrate the API. One example we discuss is protecting model reasoning against extraction used for distillation. Preserving thinking blocks across turns helps address this, but a new requirement can also break a customer's existing harness. Katelyn also describes what being part of early access programs actually looks like in practice: Customers run evaluations in their own harnesses, report surprising behavior, and sometimes pass along less formal impressions. The useful part is not just a benchmark score: it is seeing the model in environments and tasks Anthropic's own products do not cover. As we have said for 4 straight years now on the podcast , having good evals is golden. The brain and the hands Our favorite mental model in the episode is the distinction between an agent's brain and its hands. In Managed Agents , Anthropic separates the session log and harness from the sandbox that executes code. The harness can persist while an execution environment is created when needed; a failed sandbox does not have to take the whole agent session with it. We covered this in the Thariq pod : Claude Code’s Next Era — Thariq Shihipar, Anthropic — Latent Space Shipping Opus/Sonnet 5.5, Mods, Plugins, Projects, Tag while Pacing the Frontier Latent Space The same separation gives security a useful architectural property. If generated code runs in a sandbox that never receives a service credential, there is no credential in that sandbox for the code to read. The episode describes credentials held separately and attached through a proxy, alongside controls on where sandbox traffic can go. Anthropic's containment write-up describes the wider set of isolation and network controls used across its products. The distinction matters for performance too. The guests say an earlier approach put the whole coding agent in a sandbox behind an API. Starting the environment and agent added work before the first response; if the sandbox disappeared, so did the running agent. Separating the pieces allowed the platform to pursue lower latency and better reliability while keeping execution isolated. It is a helpful lens for anyone designing an agent runtime. Ask which parts need to survive, which parts execute untrusted work, and which secrets actually need to be present where code runs. The implementation will differ between products, but those questions remain useful. An agent that helps another agent remember Managed Agents also provides a base for experiments in memory and multi-agent workflows. Dreaming is simply implemented as one agent inspecting another agent's prior work and writing memories back. That makes the feature an example of building a higher-level behavior out of the same underlying managed-agent primitives. Their account of the roadmap is more nuanced than a list of features. Memory and learning remain important, but the team says more of its immediate attention has moved to safety as model launches have become harder. They also discuss keeping the base harness relatively simple, while letting developers experiment with verifiers, parallel agents and other strategies on top. Ideas mentioned for future platform capabilities should be treated as plans, not shipped promises. The conversation about evaluations follows naturally. A harness is an application, but improving one starts to resemble research: pick a goal, measure behavior, inspect failures, and iterate. The guests and hosts discuss using models to help build and analyze evaluations, while retaining enough judgment to decide whether the evaluation reflects a real user's job. Show notes Claude Opus 5.5 announcement — Anthropic's launch notes on model behavior, evaluation and pricing. Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang at Anthropic's partner summit — Anthropic identifies their platform engineering and product roles. Scaling Managed Agents: Decoupling the brain from the hands — The session, harness and sandbox architecture discussed in the episode. How Anthropic contains Claude across products — How Anthropic describes isolation, credentials and network controls across its products. Effective harnesses for long-running agents — Earlier Anthropic work on the challenge of maintaining progress across context windows. Anthropic model system cards — The company's public model evaluation and safety documentation. Anthropic S-1 breakdown — The numbers and context behind the newly recorded introduction. articles.title: Sylvia Plath on Living with the Darkness and Making Art from the Barely Bearable Lightness of Being
articles.snippet: “One has to shut off that nagging part of the mind and go on without it with bravo and philosophy.” When the twenty-two-year-old Sylvia Plath (October 27, 1932–February 11, 1963) wrote to her mother one bleak January day, both women were wading through a darkness of the soul. Science was only just beginning to hone the tools with which to begin dissecting the elemental mystery of what makes us who we are: how much of our psychology and what we experience as our personhood — whether we call it self or soul or spirit — is a product of our physical constitution, of the particular biochemical processes coursing through our particular infrastructure of matter that we experience as our body. Neuroscience was then an infant science — it still is — and the helix of heredity had just been discovered, hinting at the promise of new clarity on the ancient puzzlement of nature versus nurture, new insight into how much of our psychology is a biological inheritance and how much an ongoing composition continually revised by the confluence of chance and choice we call experience. Sylvia Plath by Rollie McKenna (Smithsonian National Portrait Gallery) Several years earlier, the teenage Plath had begun contouring her consciousness and mapping its psychological promontories, its luminous surfaces and its dark edges, rhapsodizing about the joy of living , thinking deeply about free will and what make us who we are , and composing her first tragic poem in response to a minor domestic accident. Two years before she shaded in what was becoming an all-consuming darkness in “The Disquieting Muses,” she wrote to her mother in a letter included in the posthumously collected Letters Home: Correspondence 1950–1963 ( public library ): I don’t know whether it is an hereditary characteristic, but our little family is altogether too prone to lie awake at nights hating ourselves for stupidities — technical or verbal or whatever — and to let careless, cruel remarks fester until they blossom in something like ulcer attacks — I know that during these last days I’ve been fighting an enormous battle with myself. But then, with the presence of mind and the triumph of spirit that allowed her to live through the remaining years of her life — years she filled with some of the most timelessly exquisite poetry ever written — she adds: But beyond a point, fighting only wears one out and one has to shut off that nagging part of the mind and go on without it with bravo and philosophy… Your present life is the important thing. There is a dangerous fallacy — a biological falsehood, a feebleness of empathy, an ethical failing — in the view that people who die by suicide after living with mental illness have somehow failed at life. It is one thing to feel deeply the tragedy of that loss, to rue the help not available to them in their time of struggle; it is quite another to fault the faulty instrument itself. It is impossible for any one consciousness to truly know what living inside another is like in the first place — we make art and poems and songs to try to show each other what it is like to be alive in this body-mind. But it is especially unfathomable for a mind coursing with fairly ordinary biochemistry, housed in a brain with fairy ordinary neurophysiology, to grasp what it might be like to live with a mind inflamed by ceaselessly misfiring neurotransmitters or a mind housed in a brain with a large tumor pressing against the amygdala at every moment of every hour. To survive even a single day with such a mind is no small feat. To have not only survived thirty-one years, as Sylvia Plath did, but to have filled those years with works of staggering beauty, with poems that irradiate generations of lives — that is a rare triumph of the spirit. One of Sylvia Plath’s little-known paintings . Complement with May Sarton on the cure for despair and Lorraine Hansberry — another visionary artist of Plath’s generation, who also lived and made in the darkest depths — on the most reliable antidote to depression , then hear Meryl Streep read Plath’s stunning “Morning Song” and savor a rare glimpse of the poet’s inner world through her little-known paintings . donating = loving For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years).
