articles.title: Import AI 478: Math for alignment; ProgramBench; and Mirendil shows what RSI means
articles.snippet: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now How math could help alignment: …What the “industrialization of mathematics” means for safety… AI safety startup Resolution (formerly known as Sequent, Import AI 461 ) has published work on how it has automatically formalized some mathematical statements related to statistical learning theory. Specifically, the team has autoformalized the resolution of singularities, which they believe “lays the groundwork for further automated research into the relationship between loss landscape geometry and generalization.” How they did it: I’ll skip over the math and concentrate on how they did it, which gives us some broader lessons for how people are using AI systems to push on the frontier of knowledge. A Resolution researcher “started by working with agents to develop two plans: a high-level, human-interpretable version and a detailed (112-page) plan divided into atomic steps that closely followed the existing literature,” they write. The researcher “then deputized an orchestrator agent to carry out the plan, spinning up agents to do pen-and-paper math, write Lean, and handle support functions like checking that things were staying on track… the execution phase required little scaffolding beyond the initial plan and some agent skills distilled from earlier internal autoformalization efforts.” $135k for math formalization: The work took about a week, taking “on the order of 100B input tokens (90% cache reads) and about 300 million output tokens (totaling an estimated $135,000 in token spend), and produced about 600k lines of Lean.” Now that they’ve done this, they’ve been able to accelerate some other aspects of their research: “We have already seen both benefits from autoformalization in using this library to extend parts of singular learning theory. Formalizing resolution of singularities lets us automate more of the theory, for example, to better understand sampling, and that understanding is what lets us shape how models learn, which is the goal of what we call patterning”. Why this matters – perhaps the math boom will help us make safe AI: Though frontier mathematics often seems disconnected from immediate advances in other fields, posts like this highlight how the two might converge. The key point here is that AI is making it possible to do things that were previously so unbelievably expensive and human-time-intensive that very few people did them and you couldn’t easily integrate them into the research roadmap of a startup – but that has now changed. “We expect the coming industrialization of mathematics to make possible a new, rigorous science of research automation,” Resolution writes. Read more: Formalizing Hironaka’s Resolution of Singularities (Resolution) . *** Agents can build programs from scratch: …ProgramBench goes from 0% to 18.5% performance in a few months… In a reminder of the blistering pace of AI progress, Claude Opus 5.5 (xhigh) has got a score of 18.5% on ProgramBench, a very hard benchmark that came out in May of this year – and when it came out, every tested model scored 0%. What ProgramBench is: ProgramBench tests out how well AI systems can rebuild software programs based on being given a compiled program and its documentation. Tasks include building things like language interpreters (PHP, Lua, tinycc), databases (DuckDB, SQLite), media and compression utilities (FFmpeg, zstd, xz), and developer tools (ripgrep, fzf, jq). It was very hard until it wasn’t: When it came out, the best scoring system was Claude Opus 4.7 with 0% resolved (fraction of the 200 tasks where all tests passed), and 3% almost (fraction of the 200 tasks where >95% of tests pass). Compare that to today, when Claude Opus 5.5 gets 18.5% resolved and 70.5% (!!!) almost. Why this matters – the era of ephemeral software cometh: In 2027, huge amounts of software will be built via AI systems end-to-end autonomously developing whatever they need to do for whatever tasks they’re being put to. Evals like ProgramBench give us a sense of how rapid the pace of progress is here, given we went from 0% earlier this year to 20% now. My expectation is ProgramBench is saturated by the end of 2027 (where I define saturated as some very high score on resolved, though as with most benchmarks it’s likely there’s some kind of noise ceiling here, so it might not strictly be 100%). Read more: ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch? (arXiv) . *** OpenAI illustrates why locking down AI systems is harder than you think: …Securing smart agents is like catching greased pigs… Here’s a nice post from OpenAI going over some of the things they discovered when they recently used their AI systems to ‘red team’ their own internal controls. The post goes over a number of the escapes and vulnerabilities that OpenAI’s agents found. There’s one particular example about communicating which is worth studying in detail because it tells us something about the wild cunning complexity of these systems. What they did and what they found: OpenAI “asked agents in separate microVMs, created and managed by OpenAI’s sandboxing software on shared host machines, to exchange synthetic secrets without the use of network connections or shared writable files—something that our systems are meant to prevent,” the company wrote. “The agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache: a small, fast memory that holds copies of data that applications have recently accessed. Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate. One agent encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. Another timed how long it took to reload that data, using the difference between fast and slow reads to recover the message. articles.title: Transcript: Robin Wigglesworth, on Embracing the Bond Market
articles.snippet: The transcript from this week’s MiB: Robin Wigglesworth, on Embracing the Bond Market , is below. You can stream and download our full conversation, including any podcast extras, on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , YouTube , and Bloomberg . All of our earlier podcasts on your favorite pod hosts can be found here . ~~~ MASTERS IN BUSINESS: Robin Wigglesworth Editor, FT Alphaville · Author, A Fabulous Debt: The Epic Story of How Bonds Built the Modern World Bloomberg Radio · Interview transcript · Running time 1:24 BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:00:07] I’m Barry Ritholtz. You are listening to Masters in Business on Bloomberg Radio. My extra special guest, returning to us, is Robin Wigglesworth, editor of FT Alphaville, one of my favorite sites on the web. It’s the Financial Times’ finance blog, which he runs from Oslo, Norway, with a team of writers both in London and New York. He co-hosts The Story of Money, a financial history pod, and writes the newsletter Buy the Dip. His new book, A Fabulous Debt: The Epic Story of How Bonds Built the Modern World, is out. It frames bonds as the world’s largest, most powerful financial engine. I’m halfway through it and I’ve been loving it. The conversation was fascinating. I think you’ll really enjoy it. With no further ado, my interview of Robin Wigglesworth. Robin, welcome to Bloomberg. ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:01:15] Well, it’s a massive honor to be here, so thanks for that, Barry. BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:01:19] So before we talk about the book, I want to spend a little time discussing your very interesting background. You get a bachelor’s in journalism and contemporary history from City University and then a master’s in history of international relations from the London School of Economics, focused on political Islam. Was the original career plan always journalism? ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:01:44] No, I always dreamt of being a physicist, maybe specifically an astrophysicist. BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:01:48] There is zero physics in international relations. I guess that’s really intergalactic relations. ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:01:55] Well, weirdly, you know, when you try to self-analyze it always gets a little bit weird. But I like figuring out how the world worked. And I liked physics. I loved understanding and learning about the galaxies. And I realized I was pretty good at maths and physics, up until a point I realized I would be nothing other than a mediocre physicist. BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:02:12] It’s amazing. You could be great at the secondary level, and suddenly in college, oh, those guys are really good. ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:02:18] Yeah, those guys are good. BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:02:18] I had that same experience. ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:02:19] Yeah. And it’s fine. It’s kind of knowing your limitations, what you’re good at. But journalism in many ways, I’ve kind of come to see, is similar in that you’re just figuring out the world from a different perspective. And financial journalism has at least a little bit of math, albeit not quite on the level of PhDs in physics. BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:02:36] So am I correct in saying your first gig out of LSE was Bloomberg News? Is that right? ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:02:42] No, I had one intermediate step. I was a financial journalist for a small trade mag in Dubai, and they just ingest journalists and then spit them out if they’re bad. And I didn’t know anything, but it was kind of this first awe-inspiring moment where, like, oh my God, I get paid to ask smart people about stuff. And it was so fun. I knew nothing. And luckily I didn’t embarrass myself, so they kept me around. But I quickly moved to Bloomberg because I knew that was a great place to learn. BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:03:09] So the Middle East and Dubai is a theme that comes up. You’re the Gulf correspondent in Abu Dhabi, covering the Arab Spring from both Bahrain and Libya. How do you go from that to covering finance? ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:03:24] Well, so the first job had been covering bonds. Islamic bonds, actually, sukuk. And I worked at Bloomberg as an economics and politics reporter, but also, you get roped into everything. Bloomberg’s a great place if you want to spread your wings. So I covered FX and rates a lot as well. So at the FT I was a Middle East correspondent, a Gulf correspondent, but you kind of do a bit of everything then. And it was a lot of Dubai going bankrupt. This was 2008. Dubai was having a hard time. It was fascinating. It was also covering things like labor movements in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia. But when the Arab Spring happened, I did get to cosplay as a war correspondent for a bit. And it was a wild time. I actually interviewed for a financial journalist job at the FT back in London from the army barracks of the rebel government in Benghazi. BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:04:09] Oh my God. So how do you end up covering capital markets in New York for the Financial Times? ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:04:16] Well, I went to London. I did get that job, despite the slightly bad backdrop of the Benghazi army barracks. Got the job covering capital markets for the FT in Europe. And it was the euro in crisis. And it was an incredible time. You learn so much more, so much more quickly, in a crisis. So it’s terrible for the world, great for us. And after a few years, I got moved to New York to head up the markets team there. And for me, that’s the Premier League, or the World Series. It’s New York finance. It doesn’t really get better. BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:04:51] You know, I love quoting Robert Duvall in Apocalypse Now during the financial crisis to some young analysts. There’s a line, “Someday, son, this war’s gonna end,” he says wistfully. And in the middle of a crisis, there’s very much that experience. Like, you better appreciate this, because these only come along every 20 years or so. And they’re amazing learning experiences. You experience that repeatedly. First with the Arab Spring, then with the Great Financial Crisis. What was the next big economic crisis tha

articles.title: The End of the Internet
articles.snippet: Listen to this post : Log in to listen It was the summer of 2003, just weeks before I was set to move to Taiwan, that I decided to create a blog to document my journey. I had, at that point, had a GeoCities site, a Blogspot site, a site I built in Microsoft FrontPage and hosted…somewhere, so this was my fourth swing at the blog thing (it was the seventh that ended up being Stratechery). I was intrigued by a just-released piece of software that promised a five-minute install; it was called WordPress. It did, I must confess, take me much longer than 5 minutes to install WordPress: it turned out I needed to learn how to create a MySQL database and configure PHP; once you had all of those component pieces in place, then yes, it only took 5 minutes to install! I was thinking back to those days last week when news broke that every version of PHP had a critical bug that allowed for remote code execution on the host machine; Stratechery today still runs on WordPress, but that WordPress is managed by Pressable , an Automattic company. That meant that my site was patched before the vulnerability was disclosed, and it would be crazy for me — or anyone else — to do it any other way. It’s kind of insane to think that twenty-some years ago I was doing everything by hand without having any idea what I was doing, and that it was totally fine. That’s the Internet, though: an insane invention from a time that is, sadly, gone forever. The End of Blogs 2003 was, roughly speaking, right around the beginning of the blogosphere; yes, blogs existed — Dave Winer, often considered the father of blogs, started Scripting News in 1997, after early experiments with a personal site called DaveNet ; Justin Hall started Links.net in 1994; Jorn Barger coined the term “weblog” for Robot Wisdom , also in 1997, and the influential kottke.org started in 1998 — but it was the early 2000s when blogs suddenly seemed everywhere, particularly in the political space: Talking Points Memo , Andrew Sullivan and Boing Boing launched in 2000 Instapundit , Little Green Footballs , and Dooce launched in 2001 Matt Yglesias , Daily Kos , Eschaton , The Volokh Conspiracy , Power Line , Gizmodo , Gawker , paidContent , and Daring Fireball launched in 2002 Ezra Klein , Marginal Revolution , ReadWriteWeb , and AVC launched in 2003 That political blogs featured so prominently speaks, I think, to both the power and peril of the Internet’s first transformation. Up to that point the Internet was mostly technologists, comfortable discussing the intricacies of text editors and programming languages with other nerds on BBSs, early forums, and mailing lists; it was the politically minded, however, that realized that the freedom to start your own publication that could reach everyone was a radical development. The goal was not to make money; it was to make a difference. Originally these new publications were novel; what soon became clear, however, is that they were the tip of a wave of content that would dramatically expand the web. Newspapers had influence by being geographic monopolies; early bloggers gained influence by being the first to a new medium. Ultimately, however, the real winner of the web was Google: as the amount of content became abundant, Google offered not distribution — which was free — but rather discovery; indeed, it’s because distribution was free that discovery became the most important part of the value chain. Many of those early bloggers made a decent amount of money from Google through its AdSense advertising program; by the end of the decade, however, the ads became more intrusive even as the payouts shrank, both because the inventory was limitless, and also because the most attractive ad slots were on Google Search. And so we saw one of the first examples of how the Internet fails: because everything is open, everyone has an opportunity, which means infinite competition, which is terrible for business. For many years I rued the fact I wasn’t one of those early bloggers; a decade later, however, I realized that I was actually just in time for a much more sustainable business model: subscriptions. I wrote in 2015’s Blogging’s Bright Future : It turns out, though, that there are more business models than simply advertising, as Sullivan himself sought to show. Sullivan was, for the last two years, supported by reader subscriptions to the tune of nearly one million dollars a year, and while many were skeptical of Sullivan’s efforts when he started, his ability to raise money shouldn’t have been a surprise: his is a singular voice — to put it in economic terms, Sullivan’s writing had a low elasticity of substitution — so people were happy to pay for something they couldn’t get anywhere else. Right there was the exact loyalty that Klein fears has been lost… I am, of course, acutely aware that there is a tradeoff when it comes to the subscription business model: by making something scarce, and worth paying for, you are by definition limiting your number of readers. Stratechery, though, serves a niche, and niches are best served by making more from customers who really care than from milking pennies from everyone. In short, the answer to drowning in abundance is to purposely limit your audience — to go small. That is an economic model that works, and notably, there are a lot of bloggers on that list who are using that model today. Blogging is alive and well, it’s just constrained, and thus worth paying for. The End of Social Media Google wasn’t the only Aggregator: a decade later there was a new means of discovery, which was social media. Now instead of searching for a site you could have a link shared directly to you, not just by email but on a site that served up interesting updates about whomever you chose to follow. And, for a period of time, followers could become friends. Stratechery’s fortunate timing was not just in terms of subscriptions becoming technically viable, but also the fact that Twitter was a community, not unlike

articles.title: Is our attitude up to us?
articles.snippet: If the stakes are high enough and the duration you need to keep it together is short enough, can you control your response? Because if we can do it then, we can learn to do it now. Like all skills, they take practice, preparation and effort. articles.title: 20 Favorite Children’s Books from 20 Years of The Marginalian
articles.snippet: “Anyone who writes down to children is simply wasting his time,” E.B. White insisted . “You have to write up, not down. Children are demanding. They are the most attentive, curious, eager, observant, sensitive, quick, and generally congenial readers on earth.” Both as a reader of them and as a writer of them , I have never considered “children’s books” a separate category of literature: The best children’s books are works of philosophy in disguise, shining a sidewise gleam on the fundamental questions we live with, articulating in the language of children, which is the language of great simplicity and great profundity, the most complex truths about being human. But reducing a lifetime of reading to just twenty favorite books to mark twenty years of The Marginalian was so tortuously hard that I am sneaking in another twenty under the dubious label “children’s.” THE LITTLE PRINCE Why I love it THE DARK WOOD OF THE GOLDEN BIRDS Why I love it MOOMINLAND MIDWINTER Why I love it THE LOST WORDS Why I love it BIG WOLF & LITTLE WOLF Why I love it THE WANTING MONSTER Why I love it CRY, HEART, BUT NEVER BREAK Why I love it OCEAN OF STARS Why I love it KENNY’S WINDOW Why I love it IF YOU COME TO EARTH Why I love it THIS IS A POEM THAT HEALS FISH Why I love it THE LION AND THE BIRD Why I love it THE HEART AND THE BOTTLE Why I love it THE OSBICK BIRD Why I love it ALICE’S ADVENTURES IN WONDERLAND Why I love it IN THE HALF ROOM Why I love it WHAT DO YOU KNOW? Why I love it SOMETHING ABOUT THE SKY Why I love it AT THE DROP OF A CAT Why I love it FERDINAND Why I love it (AND SOME FROM ME) donating = loving For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. articles.title: The Dark Wood of the Golden Birds: Margaret Wise Brown’s Lost Masterpiece about Mortality and the Meaning of Life, Newly Illustrated
articles.snippet: In early September 1948, a year after she rewilded the landscape of literature with Goodnight Moon , Margaret Wise Brown watched the love of her life fade to black. Michael Strange, born Blanche Oelrichs, had cast an instant spell on Margaret — outspoken, sophisticated, and self-possessed, so tall Margaret had to lift her grey-blue eyes to meet the black of Michael’s, her tall frame clad in masculine clothing she herself had designed to cling to her curves, with a musical voice unspooling from her haunting dark beauty, a deep velvet laugh, and a reputation for rarely keeping a promise. In her tight tweed pants and long-tailed blazers and oversized ties, she moved effortlessly through the sea of gloves and lace and whispering society ladies. When her wealthy family of Austrian royal lineage had found her erotic poetry embarrassing, Blanche had emancipated herself under the male nom de plume, which soon became a stage name as she strode into the theater world as playwright and actress, and eventually swelled into a total persona — the name with which she signed her letters, the name by which her intimates addressed her, the name of her self-image. Michael Strange and Margaret Wise Brown In her youth, Blanche had been named the most beautiful woman in Paris. Now, about to turn fifty-eight, Michael Strange was a ghost on a New York stage, her skin sallow, her body emaciated to the size of a child’s after refusing to let her aggressive leukemia keep her from performing. Margaret and Michael had met seven years earlier. One day on Vinalhaven — the Maine island where Margaret would spend much of her life and write most of her books — she had rowed to a lover’s cottage and found the luscious stranger sunbathing there with her lover. Soon, back in New York, she was surprised to receive a lunch invitation from Michael, who had shown up dressed in fur from head to toe, asking bold questions about her love life while sipping sherry. Margaret was thirty, Michael fifty and on her third unhappy marriage; her latest husband had never read her poetry. Both women were born in the wrong century, bent on bending it to their will; both were accidental radicals, just by living unselfconsciously; both had had affairs with Thomas Wolfe; both were at heart poets more than anything else. By the middle of the World War, they were lovers; Michael had declared that she had never loved anyone the way she loved Margaret and never would; she had promised to love her until her dying day. Late one night, Margaret’s phone rang. Michael’s voice poured in, sped up with alarm, imploring her to get into a taxi right away. Her husband had found out about their relationship and, in an era when the diagnostic manual of psychiatry classified same-sex love as a mental illness, was threatening to have her locked away in an asylum. A doctor was on his way to “diagnose” her. With her maid’s help, Michael managed to slip out through the back staircase and into the taxi as Margaret was pulling up. On the disorienting ride through the New York nocturne, they weighed their options and decided to head to the high-society women’s club Michael frequented. There, she collected herself, phoned her husband to demand a formal apology, then set the wheels in motion for a legal separation. From this point on, Michael became — to use the modern term, hard-won and ahistorical — Margaret’s partner. Soon, they were living across the hallway from each other, in a pair of twin apartments on the East End, with Margaret part nominal tenant and part unnamed wife as she was quickly becoming one of the country’s most original and beloved children’s book authors. It was a stormy love that pushed and pulled, but grafted itself onto Margaret’s being. Michael wrote adoring letters and criticized Margaret’s diction at dinner parties. She gave her a golden wishbone necklace and a ring, made her feel like she was too needy, and derided her children’s books as unsophisticated, “silly furry stories,” not Real Literature: an actress and socialite who had not published a poem in a decade and was feeling abandoned by her own muse, deriding one of the most vibrantly creative people of the past century — poet, songwriter, progressive education reformer, author of more than a hundred singularly wondrous books for the young, with which she would earn herself a little red house, a yellow convertible, and the love of millions of children; the author whom the visionary Ursula Nordstrom had no qualms calling her favorite author, despite also publishing Maurice Sendak, Shel Silverstein, and E.B. White. Even Michael’s pet name for Margaret was laced with this ambivalent mixture of affection and disdain: Bunny-no-good. And yet nobody ever knows what electrifies the infinite sky between two people, what magnetizes them together, what roils deep beneath the faint surface trails left in letters and diaries and the recollections of bystanders, what animates the long days between the islanded moments crashed by emotion and frozen in time. Margaret loved Michael with unassailable devotion, and Michael was dying. So she did the hardest thing in life — facing the death of a beloved while remaining a pillar for their passage — the best way she knew how: She wrote a love letter in the form of a children’s book. Art by Ofra Amit for The Dark Wood of the Golden Birds . Art by Ofra Amit for The Dark Wood of the Golden Birds . On the last day of spring in 1950, three years after Goodnight Moon had enraptured the world with its bright playfulness, The Dark Wood of the Golden Birds , somber and numinous with its elegiac prose, and its haunting duotone of otherworldly greens and yellows, and its simple dedication: “For Michael Strange.” Margaret asked her longtime collaborator Leonard Weisgard — one of the most prolific and beloved picture-book artists of the century — to illustrate it. articles.title: Time
articles.snippet: I think a lot about time. How we consume it, save it, enjoy it, spend it. How it can be interminably slow or rush by before you know it. Our language subtly instructs us about our concept of time: We are urged to “ savor the moment ”; we want to “ be present.” Even store clerks bid us to “ have a good day ”, as if you control whether this 24-hour period will be good or not. You can, of course, try your best to have a good day , and sometimes succeed – unless the universe has other plans for you.1 I’ve always been fascinated by time; maybe that’s why I was so intrigued by watches as a kid. A few recent events have me thinking about time more than usual: a big birthday, a loss, other events … ~~~ Age I never had a midlife crisis. Perhaps it was too cliché. Big round birthdays and aging never bothered me. The only experience I had relative to age was waking up on the morning of my 60th birthday and immediately thinking, “ Start of the fourth quarter, down by 7 – you’re still in this thing, but lots to do. Get busy !” The result was a new book , some personal projects, financial and estate planning, and less procrastination on major purchases, travel, and activities I had been putting off for no good reason. As an immortal, I would get around to them eventually. Once the 19-year-old in me admitted immortality was no longer operative, I suddenly felt an urgency to check off some boxes. No, not a bucket list , just a short inventory of unfulfilled desires I suddenly felt the urge to make happen. Hey, wait a second… ~~~ Impermanence Our house developed an exterior leak that dripped into the basement. To prep for the contractors, we cleared out a lot of accumulated junk. The big surprise: 6 MacBooks dating back to the 2000s. Six! Each one was a thing : expensive, useful, important, yet oh so temporary. We were warned: “ Don’t throw away old laptops unless you removed the hard drives! ” Looking at these old, battered MacBooks, I remember the excitement of buying them: Faster, better, improved! When we buy something new, we forget it will eventually wear out, get damaged, become less useful, get replaced or discarded. Everything! The second law of thermodynamics is a bitch. ~~~ Illusion Here’s something you might not have considered : Time , at least as an objective concept outside human consciousness, doesn’t exist. It’s (mostly) a human creation; no chrono particles, no celestial timekeeper, no physical mechanism governs time’s passage. Our experience is an illusion, a function of our sensory inputs colliding with our consciousness… Physics recognizes Time is a useful construct, a handy artifice for comparing forces relative to one another. “ T ” in equations is time as a dimension between other vectors. You use it to measure speed or distance, but mostly relative to each other. Every measure of time seems to quantify only an object’s motion, whether it’s the vibration of a Cesium atom or the hands on a clock.2 I wonder: Does Time exist independently of us, conscious beings? Without us, does the relative motion of objects in 3-dimensional space include time – or is that simply a convenient human assumption? 3 The flow of time seems especially illusory: The sense of RIGHT HERE AND NOW, the intersection of THIS instant (T) and THIS location (X, Y, & Z), is moving forward, a present “now” that advances tick by tick, second by second, and millennia by millennia. I struggle to believe this is anything other than the human mind trying to make sense of the experiential universe… Our experience of Time, which changes so radically over our lives, is an illusion. ~~~ Money is Time I contributed a chapter to the new book “ How I Invest My Money Volume Two ,” which was published this week. Excellent financial advice needs specific personalization; I wanted to write something universal. My chapter, titled “ Money Is Time ,” is a tight 860 words, but has three concepts worth sharing: First, Money is society’s measure of the economic contributions you make with your time (including effort, expertise, insight, skill, etc., which are themselves functions of time). Second, we all get precisely 24 hours a day. Each of us is born wealthy in time, with endless, infinite hours, days, weeks, months, and years, which we fritter away when young. Later in life, we learn that time is our stock in trade. And third, Money IS Time. Every purchase you make is an investment of your insultingly limited time. The days may be long, but the decades are short. Keep this front of mind as you spend your finite supply of time. ~~~ Time Travel As a sci-fi fan, I’ve sat through more than my fair share of time-travel flicks. Screenwriters and novelists seem to ignore two issues. The first is Location : When you travel back in time, the planet you’re standing on will have moved – millions or billions of miles away. The Earth orbits the Sun at 66,600 mph; the Sun makes a 260-million-year route around the Milky Way at 515,000 mph; even the Earth’s rotation is 1,040 mph. You must surmise your position relative to the galactic expansion at 515,000 mph, despite its occasional changes in acceleration. 4 In total, we are moving at 828,000 mph. Time travel for a century, and you space travel 725 billion miles (best of luck calculating that precisely). Off by a trillionth of a %, e.g., ~three-quarters of a mile, you materialize inside Earth’s crust (deadly) or nearly 4,000 feet in the air before gravity ends you. Greater errors deliver you into the vacuum of space. My second issue is the Arrow of Time . It annoys me to send people into a nondeterministic future that hasn’t happened yet. I don’t buy the thesis of a Universe as a block of past, present, and future all occurring at once – it lacks causality.5 In my version of time travel, you can go into the past, but only to return to the point from which you departed. But you cannot visit the Restaurant at the End of the Universe because it hasn’t happened yet. Between now and then, many things wil

articles.title: Seam Cutter
articles.snippet: Tool: Seam Cutter I built this weird and very specific cropping tool - it lets you create a horizontal or vertical cut across an image, then slide the two sides relative to each other. Effectively it lets you crop out a section in the middle of an image. I wanted this because I often use Tailor on my iPhone to stitch several screenshots together into lot long image, but sometimes I find myself wanting to crop out a section in the middle - to redact an irrelevant prompt from a transcript, for example. articles.title: Podcast: Kimi K3.1 Pro, the new cyber reality, and Muse musings
articles.snippet: We — Nathan and Florian — wanted to discuss all the messy trade-offs of a busy week in AI and ask all the pressing questions like: Why did Kimi K3.1 Pro have a mixed reaction with such incredible benchmarks? Will it be adopted? Were we wrong about the risks of open-weight models and cybersecurity? Why do cyber experts discuss recent events so differently than AI experts? What comes next in the few months? What will change our minds? We will write more about this subject, but wanted to bring you behind the curtain as we aspire to quickly learn more about the cybersecurity industry and trends across the last few years that have been leading us today. We conclude the podcast with some lighter topics, from Muse-maxing to excitement in still hiring junior technical talent. Please send us questions and topics, as we plan to record more of these podcasts going forward. Share Listen on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , and wherever you get your podcasts . For other Interconnects podcasts, go here . YouTube ↓ Chapters 00:00 Kimi K3.1 Reaction 08:15 Kimi’s open-weight cyber principles 11:23 You can hack everything era 15:54 PHP2Shell, LiteLLM, and the new internet 24:00 Abliterated APIs, safeguards, and trusted access 31:41 Anthropic not hiring juniors employees 36:16 Florian’s Muse addiction 45:30 Wrap-up Links we discuss My thread with Dean Ball about the “boy who cried wolf” story of the frontier labs Kimi K3.1 Pro announcement blog Kimi K3.1 Pro on Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index Kimi K3.1 on Artificial Analysis defensive cyber benchmarks Program Bench Open-weight Mythos would’ve been fine take PHP “hasn’t caused a disaster yet” update Abliteration.ai serving abliterated models API Morph serving abliterated DeepSeek via API Joshua Saxe’s Substack on AI and cybersecurity Azeem Azhar, “The internet’s Wuhan moment” Anthropic, “How employment is changing at Anthropic” LiteLLM security incident report Transcript 00:00:00 Nathan Lambert: We are back with another Interconnects podcast. We are with Florian, eval guy, recently moved to SF. Florian, is Kimi K3.1 Pro , name is a mouthful, going to live up to the benchmark scores, for example on Artificial Analysis , or where is it going to land? 00:00:17 Florian Brand: In the past, the Kimi models always lived up to the expectations, but this release is kind of weird compared to the others. I think it is also partially because they are becoming more professional, and the previous model drops were kind of out of nowhere. This time, which also got some criticism, they launched a bigger social media campaign, which allegedly also involved paying people to post about the model without disclosing. 00:00:56 Nathan Lambert: I think a lot of companies do this and tell you not to mention it, but it’s a mess. It’s bad form. No company should do it. Essentially, one person tweeted a screenshot of the press instructions for Kimi that said, “Don’t say this is a paid promotion.” And to my knowledge, no one has corroborated it after that. 00:01:15 Florian Brand: Yeah, and there are right now a few of these model launches, including by American companies, that are just very obviously astroturfed. We have seen launches where it’s thousands of retweets and a few hundred likes, because it works so well to get the attention. Some of them disclose that it is a paid ad while others don’t. But in general, we have seen the professionalization of model launches over time, and pretty quickly. A year ago, everyone just dropped the model, then patched vLLM afterwards, so no one was actually able to run any of the open models for a while. Now you get all the inference frameworks on day one, you get all the inference providers on day one. Or, which is also what we see more and more, the model creator has a few weeks of exclusive access before they release the weights. And that’s also what’s happening with K3.1 Pro. I think it’s two weeks of exclusive access before they release the model weights. 00:02:38 Nathan Lambert: They said the weights would come out by November 4th. And the headline things... I don’t know if I’m going to be able to share screen. I don’t have this set up on this computer. But the headline is this Artificial Analysis number where it’s ahead of GPT-6 Astra. And then if you look at the Kimi K3.1 blog, they have their headline numbers, which are really strong, and then they also have some numbers later on which seem a bit more jagged. I think it was Terminal-Bench Science , which is 20 points behind GPT-6 Astra. I think there were a few others, like ProgramBench . Do you know Terminal-Bench Science and ProgramBench? Are any of these things that people think are important benchmarks for frontier models? Or how do you explain the fact that on Artificial Analysis the model is top, what, three, four? It’s the two latest Claude 5.5 models, Muse Wonder Full, and then Kimi K3.1, which looks crazy. It just looks like totally crazy scores, and I think everybody is still surprised by it. But then there’s this long tail of details that you use to evaluate a model now. I had posted a thread on Twitter of, “What are people’s impressions?” And there’s a lot of people that are like, “This seems not great,” and then some people that are like, “Yeah, it’s fine.” I don’t know, there’s a mixed bag. Relative to K3, which I think was pretty unanimously, this feels like a big model and the post-training seemed a little bit undercooked for that. Maybe this is just a tiny bit RL fried. We’ll see where we land. 00:04:26 Florian Brand: For the benchmarks, one of the things is that the benchmarks that are right now used by Artificial Analysis, they will post their new version probably very soon after we release this podcast. 00:04:43 Nathan Lambert: We can’t tell you the exact date, but both of us know. 00:04:48 Florian Brand: In general, the Artificial Analysis benchmarks are rather short in terms of time horizon, whereas something like ProgramBench is really long and also very explorative.

articles.title: 10 Sunday Reads
articles.snippet: Avert your eyes! My Sunday morning look at incompetence, corruption, and policy failures: • People Trying to Quietly Quit MAGA : There’s a familiar ritual that happens every time an authoritarian movement begins to collapse. The supporters disappear. Not physically. Psychologically. They scrub the evidence, rewrite the timeline, and emerge on the other side with a story they’ve rehearsed just enough to almost believe. “I never really supported him.” “I just voted against the Democrats.” “I don’t talk about politics anymore.” This is happening right now across America. The yard signs are coming down. The hats are going into drawers. The Facebook posts are being deleted. And millions of people who spent a decade loudly and publicly cheering for cruelty are quietly trying to exit the building before someone turns the lights on.​ ( Lucas Bean ) • Tesla profits drop 43% in Q3 Tesla’s once-booming energy storage business also shrank in Q3 2026. ( Ars Technica ) see also SpaceX and Tesla Are Already Joined at the Hip. What a Formal Merger Would Mean. : Musk says both boards have formed committees to evaluate a merger. The Journal on two companies that have shared resources and personnel for two decades. ( Wall Street Journal ) ​• Options ETFs Are Booming. Beware of the Trade-Offs. : Born of the zero-rate era, buffer and covered-call ETFs now hold close to $300 billion. Barron’s on what skittish investors give up for the monthly income. These pricey, complex strategies appeal to income-hungry and skittish investors—but some can cap your upside and leave you exposed to market downsides. ( Barron’s ) ​• The Art of the Deal: Jared Kushner’s Hacked Phone Revealed More Than $700 Million in Transfers : Matthew Cole: in 2020 a source said the Dutch government had hacked Kushner’s phone and watched him move hundreds of millions through a Dubai account funded from Azerbaijan, with transfers to a warlord, a mercenary and a one-time hit man. It sounded preposterous. And yet. ( Vanity Fair ) See also : Kushner Phone Hack Reveals How Middle East Dictators Bought Him Off ( The New Republic ) • Fox News Is Making You Dumber : Fox News viewers scored lowest. Not just among cable news viewers. Among everyone. People who reported consuming no news at all answered more questions correctly than people whose primary news source was Fox News. ​Lucas Bean revisits a 2012 Fairleigh Dickinson PublicMind poll on how well Americans know current events, and what it found about Fox viewers. ( Lucas Bean ) ​• The Ford Foundation Charts New Course to Support Preconditions for Thriving Democracies : The foundation’s new strategy refocuses its mission on democratic values, fundamental freedoms and inclusive economies worldwide. ( Ford Foundation ) See also Judge J. Michael Luttig. The Ford Foundation and Its President Heather Gerken Answer America’s Call : The $18 billion Foundation’s new strategy is anchored in protecting and strengthening the core principles that sustain America’s Democracy and Rule of Law. ( J. Michael Luttig ) ​• When Idaho Banned Abortion, OB-GYNs Fled. The Doctors Who Stayed Are Cracking. : Lisa Lerer opens with a mother who traveled two hours to deliver her baby in Moscow, Idaho. From childbirth to miscarriages, women’s health care in the state has become increasingly dangerous. ( New York Times ) ​• The Hidden History of American Healthcare: How Prudential Killed Healthcare for All : Part two of the Frederick Hoffman story: the industry playbook against universal coverage was written in 1917 and is still in use. Part two of the Frederick Hoffman story. The industry playbook against universal coverage was written in 1917, and it’s still in use… ( Hartmann Report ) • The Fatal Flaw of 911 : Rebecca Neusteter, author of a new book on the emergency system, on why the number every American knows so often sends police to mental-health calls. ( The Marshall Project ) ​• Trump Is Encouraging Airlines to Scam Passengers in Every Way Possible : Ross Rosenfeld builds on a Times investigation showing how the administration has halted or rolled back Biden-era efforts to expand airline passengers’ rights. One more annoyance you might not realize is his doing. Biden cracked down on carriers’ junk fees and hidden fees, flight delays and cancellations, and deceptive pricing. Trump is undoing all of that progress. ( New Republic ) see also How the Trump Administration Is Eroding Airline Passengers’ Rights : Under Sean Duffy, the Transportation Department has worked to roll back consumer protections. Passenger advocates say the changes favor airlines. ( New York Times ) Video of the day : I Investigated Flock Cameras. Then Police Came to My Door. (Anthony Sistilli) Be sure to check out our Masters in Business interview this weekend with Robin Wigglesworth; he is editor of FT Alphaville , the Financial Times’ finance blog, which he runs from Oslo with a team of writers in London and New York. He also co-hosts The Story of Money , the FT’s financial history podcast, with Gillian Tett, and writes the Substack Buy The Dip . His new book, “ A Fabulous Debt: The Epic Story of How Bonds Built the Modern World ” was just published to outstanding reviews. articles.title: Hospitality in the mirror
articles.snippet: Danny Meyer and Will Guidara have each written fabulous books about hospitality. They missed one thing. The customers who get the most authentic and lasting hospitality are the ones who deserve it. And the ones who deserve it actually enjoy it the most. Extraordinary hospitality offers someone more human effort and delight than they expect. You’re not entitled to something human simply because you paid for your ticket or your table. The kids who show up on Halloween get a piece of candy, but the ritual ends there. When someone with a great costume, or singing a song or simply creating a bit of connection or magic shows up, it’s different. That’s the one we remember, the reason we answered the door and our chance to show up and return the energy. Or even a full-sized ethical chocolate bar. For too long, the entitled customer has demanded emotional labor without offering support or sustenance in return. It’s exhausting and unfair, for both parties. When you’re the best customer we’ve had all day, it’s likely we’ll be the host you’re hoping for. And the best part is, that no matter how it turns out, simply trying to be the best customer of the day is its own reward. We care because we can.

articles.title: 20 Favorite Books from 20 Years of The Marginalian
articles.snippet: It is a beautiful dream, that there is something out there to instruct you how to live — a secret handed down by your parents or your teachers, a system like liberal arts education or cognitive behavioral therapy, a slogan held up by your heroes declaring the answer to the bottomless question of why you are here. Whenever you wake up, however you wake up, you find yourself on a path no one else can walk for you, a path you must make by walking. Still, you can find signposts that keep you from losing your way in loneliness. “You think your pain and your heartbreak are unprecedented in the history of the world,” James Baldwin wrote , “but then you read.” In celebrating twenty years of The Marginalian — this ongoing record of learning how to live written in marginalia on the books I have read — I have attempted the impossible: to distill a lifetime of reading into the twenty books that have served as the most enduring signposts, apart from those I have written (which always both shape and are shaped by a writer’s life more profoundly than any books read). Here they are, in no particular order. LEAVES OF GRASS (WALT WHITMAN) Why I love it A RESPONSIBILITY TO AWE (REBECCA ELSON) Some of why I love it EINSTEIN’S DREAMS (ALAN LIGHTMAN) Why I love it THE LOG FROM THE SEA OF CORTEZ (JOHN STEINBECK) Why I love it THE ABUNDANCE (ANNIE DILLARD) Some of why I love it THE RIVER OF CONSCIOUSNESS (OLIVER SACKS) Some of why I love it THE BOOK OF DELIGHTS (ROSS GAY) Why I love it WILLARD GIBBS (MURIEL RUKEYSER) Why I love it THE DICTIONARY OF OBSCURE SORROWS (JOHN KOENIG) Why I love it THE FRAGILE SPECIES (LEWIS THOMAS) Why I love it THE SOURCE OF SELF-REGARD (TONI MORRISON) Some of why I love it THE STAR THROWER (LOREN EISELEY) Why I love it EXISTENTIALISTS AND MYSTICS (IRIS MURDOCH) Some of why I love it UPSTREAM (MARY OLIVER) Why I love it CHAOS (JAMES GLEICK) Why I love it THE WAVE IN THE MIND (URSULA K. LE GUIN) Some of why I love it NOTHING PERSONAL (JAMES BALDWIN) Why I love it THANKS (RACHEL HÉBERT) Why I love it CONSOLATIONS (DAVID WHYTE) Some of why I love it A MADMAN DREAMS OF TURING MACHINES (JANNA LEVIN) Why I love it (AND SOME FROM ME) donating = loving For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a donation . Your support makes all the difference. newsletter The Marginalian has a free weekly newsletter. It comes out on Sundays and offers the week’s most inspiring reading. Here’s what to expect . Like? articles.title: The Baloney Detection Kit: Carl Sagan’s Timeless Tenets of Critical Thinking
articles.snippet: Necessary cognitive fortification against propaganda, pseudoscience, and general falsehood. Carl Sagan (November 9, 1934–December 20, 1996) was many things — a cosmic sage , voracious reader , hopeless romantic , and brilliant philosopher . But above all, he endures as our era’s greatest patron saint of reason and critical thinking, a master of the vital balance between skepticism and openness . In The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark ( public library ) — the same indispensable volume that gave us Sagan’s timeless meditation on science and spirituality , published mere months before his death in 1996 — Sagan shares his secret to upholding the rites of reason, even in the face of society’s most shameless untruths and outrageous propaganda. In a chapter titled “The Fine Art of Baloney Detection,” Sagan reflects on the many types of deception to which we’re susceptible — from psychics to religious zealotry to paid product endorsements by scientists, which he held in especially low regard, noting that they “betray contempt for the intelligence of their customers” and “introduce an insidious corruption of popular attitudes about scientific objectivity.” (Cue in PBS’s Joe Hanson on how to read science news .) But rather than preaching from the ivory tower of self-righteousness, Sagan approaches the subject from the most vulnerable of places — having just lost both of his parents, he reflects on the all too human allure of promises of supernatural reunions in the afterlife, reminding us that falling for such fictions doesn’t make us stupid or bad people, but simply means that we need to equip ourselves with the right tools against them. Through their training, scientists are equipped with what Sagan calls a “baloney detection kit” — a set of cognitive tools and techniques that fortify the mind against penetration by falsehoods: The kit is brought out as a matter of course whenever new ideas are offered for consideration. If the new idea survives examination by the tools in our kit, we grant it warm, although tentative, acceptance. If you’re so inclined, if you don’t want to buy baloney even when it’s reassuring to do so, there are precautions that can be taken; there’s a tried-and-true, consumer-tested method. But the kit, Sagan argues, isn’t merely a tool of science — rather, it contains invaluable tools of healthy skepticism that apply just as elegantly, and just as necessarily, to everyday life. By adopting the kit, we can all shield ourselves against clueless guile and deliberate manipulation. Sagan shares nine of these tools: Wherever possible there must be independent confirmation of the “facts.” Encourage substantive debate on the evidence by knowledgeable proponents of all points of view. Arguments from authority carry little weight — “authorities” have made mistakes in the past. They will do so again in the future. Perhaps a better way to say it is that in science there are no authorities; at most, there are experts. Spin more than one hypothesis. If there’s something to be explained, think of all the different ways in which it could be explained. Then think of tests by which you might systematically disprove each of the alternatives. What survives, the hypothesis that resists disproof in this Darwinian selection among “multiple working hypotheses,” has a much better chance of being the right answer than if you had simply run with the first idea that caught your fancy. Try not to get overly attached to a hypothesis just because it’s yours. It’s only a way station in the pursuit of knowledge. Ask yourself why you like the idea. Compare it fairly with the alternatives. See if you can find reasons for rejecting it. If you don’t, others will. Quantify. If whatever it is you’re explaining has some measure, some numerical quantity attached to it, you’ll be much better able to discriminate among competing hypotheses. What is vague and qualitative is open to many explanations. Of course there are truths to be sought in the many qualitative issues we are obliged to confront, but finding them is more challenging. If there’s a chain of argument, every link in the chain must work (including the premise) — not just most of them. Occam’s Razor. This convenient rule-of-thumb urges us when faced with two hypotheses that explain the data equally well to choose the simpler. Always ask whether the hypothesis can be, at least in principle, falsified. Propositions that are untestable, unfalsifiable are not worth much. Consider the grand idea that our Universe and everything in it is just an elementary particle — an electron, say — in a much bigger Cosmos. But if we can never acquire information from outside our Universe, is not the idea incapable of disproof? You must be able to check assertions out. Inveterate skeptics must be given the chance to follow your reasoning, to duplicate your experiments and see if they get the same result. Just as important as learning these helpful tools, however, is unlearning and avoiding the most common pitfalls of common sense. Reminding us of where society is most vulnerable to those, Sagan writes: In addition to teaching us what to do when evaluating a claim to knowledge, any good baloney detection kit must also teach us what not to do. It helps us recognize the most common and perilous fallacies of logic and rhetoric. Many good examples can be found in religion and politics, because their practitioners are so often obliged to justify two contradictory propositions. He admonishes against the twenty most common and perilous ones — many rooted in our chronic discomfort with ambiguity — with examples of each in action: ad hominem — Latin for “to the man,” attacking the arguer and not the argument (e.g., The Reverend Dr. Smith is a known Biblical fundamentalist, so her objections to evolution need not be taken seriously ) argument from authority (e.g., President Richard Nixon should be re-elected because he has a secret plan to end the war in South

articles.title: MiB: Robin Wigglesworth, on Embracing the Bond Market
articles.snippet: This week, I speak with Robin Wigglesworth, editor of FT Alphaville , the Financial Times’ finance blog, which he runs from Oslo with a team of writers in London and New York. He joined the FT from Bloomberg News in 2008, where he had covered Nordic economics, and went on to serve as the paper’s Gulf correspondent, capital markets correspondent, deputy head of fastFT, US markets editor, and global finance correspondent before taking over Alphaville in 2022. He also co-hosts The Story of Money , the FT’s financial history podcast, with Gillian Tett, and writes the Substack Buy The Dip . His first book, Trillions: How a Band of Wall Street Renegades Invented the Index Fund and Changed Finance Forever , was the subject of our first conversation in 2021. We discuss why the bond market, not the stock market, is the real engine of the global economy, and how debt built the modern world, from 12th-century Venice to today’s Treasury basis trades. We talk about why the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage is “a miracle of the modern world,” how the market absorbed the Liberty Loans, the rise of the rating agencies, and the invention of money market funds and credit default swaps. We also cover quantitative easing, the Fed, and the question everyone keeps asking: when should we actually start worrying about US debt? Robin’s answer is more nuanced than either the doom-mongers or the dismissers would have you believe. His new book, “ A Fabulous Debt: The Epic Story of How Bonds Built the Modern World ,” was just published to outstanding reviews. (The title comes from Thomas Macaulay, skewering the debt scolds who had repeatedly predicted that Britain’s war borrowing would spell its doom — and were repeatedly wrong.) A list of his favorite books is here ; A transcript of our conversation is available here Tuesday. You can stream and download our full conversation, including any podcast extras, on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , YouTube , and Bloomberg . All of our earlier podcasts on your favorite pod hosts can be found here . Be sure to check out our Masters in Business next week with Rich Steinmeier , Chief Executive Officer of LPL Financial Holdings Inc. (Nasdaq: LPLA), the largest independent broker-dealer in the country. 32,000 advisors and $2.4 trillion in brokerage and advisory assets. CEO since October 2024. articles.title: Building Reasoning Models from the Ground Up: A Full Video Course
articles.snippet: I have written a lot about reasoning models here over the last two years on Ahead of AI, including a recent article on mechanisms to control reasoning effort levels in contemporary LLMs . Reasoning models are still as relevant as ever. In fact, almost all current-generation LLMs today are reasoning models or offer a reasoning mode. For those who are interested in how reasoning models work, including inference scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation, I wrote my recent Build Reasoning Model (From Scratch), which implements these from the ground up in PyTorch, which, in my experience, is still the best way to understand and learn how things really work. Now, in the last few months, I also sat down and recorded accompanying lectures I wanted to share with you. So, below, you will find eight reasoning model-from-scratch coding videos (11 hours of content). We start with a pre-trained LLM and implement methods to evaluate and improve it in Python and PyTorch. So, if you enjoyed my Coding LLMs from the Ground Up course last year, this is essentially the sequel (but you can also watch it without the prior course as a prerequisite). I’m currently taking a short break and will be back soon with more exciting LLM research roundups next month. In the meantime, I hope you enjoy coding along! How LLMs, reasoning models, and agents relate and fit together As a small side note, and since I often get asked how reasoning models relate to today’s AI agents, here’s a short section on this before getting started with the videos. A reasoning model is essentially an upgrade from a conventional LLM, that is, adding more post-training via reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (and optionally inference scaling techniques) to make it more capable of solving more challenging problems. Classically, reasoning models are developed for math and code, but the capabilities can generalize to other problem domains as well. A reasoning model then functions as the engine inside an agent harness, where the agent harness is a software or tooling framework around the LLM/reasoning model to tackle even more challenging problems (bigger coding tasks, travel booking, and all other sorts of personal assistant tasks). The task of the harness is sophisticated context management and giving the LLM access to tools. Figure 1: An engine analogy for conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses. Figure from my Components of a Coding Agent article. In this analogy depicted in the figure above, the model is the engine, and the agent harness adds the machinery that lets us use it for various things (as an upgrade from a simple chatbot interface). An agent can use either a conventional LLM or a reasoning model, but reasoning models are the more typical choice as they are more capable. (As mentioned above, most current-gen LLMs are reasoning models with variable reasoning effort settings.) So, the bottom line is that reasoning models, as the “engine,” remain an important part of understanding modern LLM agents. The resources accompanying these topics shown above are: The Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) book and videos The Build A Reasoning Model (From Scratch) book (and videos below) The Components of a Coding Agent article on Substack The videos below focus on developing the reasoning model that can power such a system. Scope and prerequisites The reasoning-from-scratch videos focus on a small pre-trained Qwen3 model, where we implement the reasoning methods ourselves in Python and PyTorch. Starting with a pre-trained model lets us focus on the interesting part: evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation. Regarding the prerequisites, I recommend being comfortable with Python and PyTorch. I designed the reasoning materials as standalone content, so the previous Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch) content is recommended but not strictly required. Compute-resource-wise, you can work through the early text-generation and evaluation examples on a CPU. For the later experiments, especially training, a GPU makes the work much more practical. The first video covers the setup and some more recommendations; the repository also includes hardware and environment recommendations . Figure 2: An overview of the topics being covered. The companion book These videos accompany my book, Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) . If you like to read through the explanation in more detail and at your own pace, work through exercises, and so on, I recommend the book as a companion here. For the most in-depth learning experience, my suggestion is to read a chapter, work through its code alongside the corresponding video, and then try the exercises. The book is available from Manning and Amazon , and the print edition is in color! Figure 3: A random excerpt from the Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) print book. Thank you to everyone who has picked up a copy or recommended it to a friend. Your support helps me keep creating these materials. The videos As a last, quick side note before getting to the main videos below: For a shorter, more conceptual overview, I also recommend my AI Reasoning Models course on LinkedIn Learning (it should be free for 24h when accessing it via the link there, which shouldn’t then require a LinkedIn Premium subscription). The course is about 90 minutes and explains how reasoning models work, covering the main ideas behind inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation. It’s a good optional preview if you’d like the main ideas without working through the full implementations below. To get to the main part of this article, here are the eight main lecture videos. 1. Motivation and code setup The first video starts with an explanation of the relationship between conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agents. Next, the main topic of the video is setting up the coding environment. This includes installing the Python and PyTorch dependencie

articles.title: Caveman leadership and the CDO*
articles.snippet: We don’t have written records, but I’m imagining that groups of cavemen made decisions around the fire in largely the same way we run sophisticated organizations today. About a hundred years ago, three disciplines helped create the modern world: Scientific management used a stopwatch and the assembly line to relentlessly improve the productivity of the industrial age. Scientific advertising brought measurement and rigor to the work of creating ads and buying media. And engineering brought physics and the scientific method to everything we build. Bridges don’t fall down, computer chips get faster and cheaper and the things we make rarely break. But the bosses still do what they always did. They place comfort and convenience over effectiveness. If the hard-working people in any other part of the organization approached their work the way they do, it wouldn’t last. One estimate is that the direct labor cost of time spent in meetings at a Fortune 500 company is over a quarter of a billion dollars a year. Per company. And yet, meetings occur regularly, with no measurable outputs. Few people do the reading or prep, and many show up late or uninformed. The room isn’t designed for the purpose it’s being used for, and no one is taking notes or sending out follow-up action requests. There’s rarely an interlocutor–a neutral moderator who asks questions, guides the conversation and leads the group to a decision. People are rarely given feedback on their meeting productivity, and aren’t encouraged to get training or improve their skills. You’ve probably been to a thousand meetings. How many can you remember that achieved what could have happened with that much time and talent invested? In my experience at large organizations, the physical dynamic in the room is often left to the facilities person who ran the AV cart in high school or the office supply vendor who was asked to fill a square room with furniture that would serve many purposes. That’s not how we invest in an assembly line or a semiconductor fab… And many decisions, if implemented, remain unexamined. There’s little time or focus invested in learning from what came before, and no one is keeping track of whether the loud voices are usually right. Famous CEOs shoot from the hip, and seem to think that wrong action fast is better than thoughtfully doing the right thing tomorrow. Corporate culture usually pushes people to avoid speaking up, to prize comfort over progress, and to support the status quo unless there’s an emergency. We either invite too many or not enough people into group decisions, and end up using superficial or extraneous information to make choices. We reject a job applicant because they had parsley in their teeth, didn’t go to a famous college or they don’t look like us. Deniability often seems more important than progress. We use easy proxies and measures instead of the ones that really matter. And we repeat patterns that worked with the old systems, but make no sense with the new ones. *The job of the Chief Decision Officer, then, isn’t to make decisions. It’s to create the conditions for the organization to do a better job of it. Not only at a Fortune 500 company, but at a thriving non-profit, a government agency or a small start-up. Surgeons scrub before entering the OR. It’s hygienic, but also a ritual. It reminds them that this place is special, it has a purpose, rules and outcomes. Don’t come in if you’re not prepared to do your part. The CDO ought to establish the same approach for the way we make decisions and take action on those decisions.

articles.title: [AINews] Kimi 3.1 Pro 104BA-2.8T: Fable-5.1-Class Open Weights narrows Closed-AI lead to 1 month... and Pro Highspeed API with 2-3× speed
articles.snippet: 2 months ago we covered Z.ai CEO Prof Jie Tang’s prediction that we’d get a Fable-class open weights model by year end . 2 weeks ago Meta achieved a Fable-class model in closed source , but, with 2.5 months left to go, we finally got it - a 2.8T open weights model beating Fable 5.1, not just Fable 5, at that: View post on X ↗ with even better efficiency: View post on X ↗ You can tell Kimi is proud of their latest model by how fancy their landing page is: As usual we don’t get much research detail - the update is somewhat similar to Z.ai ’s 5.2-5.3 bump - a minor version bump for a lot more post-training: Kimi K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3, with substantially larger post-training compute. To enable large-scale joint RL across hundreds of downstream domains , we optimized every layer of the stack — the RL framework, long-context inference, training efficiency, sandbox infrastructure, rollout scheduling, and a shared platform for environment quality checks — so that each increment of RL compute delivers stable, predictable returns. As a result, K3.1 Pro achieves consistent gains in every domain. AI News for 10/22/2026-10/23/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap Top Story: Kimi K3.1 Pro launch and reactions What happened Moonshot launched Kimi K3.1 Pro with near-frontier independent benchmark results, a substantial increase in model size, and an open-weight release promised for November 4, 2026. The model: Moonshot describes K3.1 Pro as a multimodal, “3T-class” mixture-of-experts model with 2.8 trillion total parameters, 104 billion active parameters, and a 1-million-token context window . Its advertised strengths include full-project coding, Blender/CAD work, financial modeling, and long-running agents. @Kimi_Moonshot Availability: Standard and Highspeed versions launched across Kimi’s website/app, Kimi Work, Kimi Code, and API. Moonshot claims Highspeed preserves intelligence while generating output 2–3× faster ; the official-account summary says it costs twice as much . The launch also includes Kimi Hosted Agents , a managed harness with a 24/7 execution environment for long-running work and multi-agent collaboration. @ZhihuFrontier , @ZhihuFrontier Independent general-capability result: Artificial Analysis placed K3.1 Pro fourth on its Intelligence Index, scoring 55 , behind Opus 5.5 at 58 and Sonnet 5.5 and Muse Wonder Full at 56. Its strongest improvements were agentic rather than uniformly distributed across knowledge and science tests. @ArtificialAnlys Independent coding result: Arena placed it #8 in Code Arena: WebDev, at 1,692 points , up nine places and 37 points over Kimi K3. Moonshot returned to Arena’s top four labs . @arena Independent cyber result: Despite deliberately reducing cyber-related training, it subsequently scored 64% on Artificial Analysis’ Cyber Index —the highest publicly accessible result and second overall, behind trusted-access GPT-6 Sol Daybreak Blue at 69%. @ArtificialAnlys The reaction split: Enthusiasm about a prospective open-weight frontier contender was followed by concerns about inference economics, weaker results on some interactive tasks, benchmark presentation, and allegations of undisclosed paid promotion. These are distinct issues: benchmark quality does not establish deployment economics, and promotional misconduct allegations do not establish model capability. @simonw , @maxbittker , @kimmonismus Release status, architecture, and what “open” means here At launch, the API was available; the weights were not . Moonshot’s announcement promises weights by November 4, 2026 . The supplied tweets do not establish the eventual license, redistribution conditions, commercial-use restrictions, checkpoint precision, or complete inference requirements. Consequently, “soon-to-be open-weight” is more precise than the “OSS” or “open source” language used in several reactions. Artificial Analysis explicitly recorded the weights as unpublished. @Kimi_Moonshot , @ArtificialAnlys The release sequence generated confusion: Early reports predicted a release “today” and potentially the strongest open-weight model, explicitly on rumors/leaks ; a follow-up reiterated positive hearsay. Neither was an evaluation. @kimmonismus , @kimmonismus Teasers triggered speculation about November 5 , including whether Moonshot would monetize website access before publishing weights. The official announcement subsequently specified November 4 . @scaling01 , @scaling01 , @bigeagle_xd Initial users reported availability on kimi.com before kimi.ai ; another later reported obtaining access. These are rollout observations, not evidence of a lasting regional restriction. @teortaxesTex , @teortaxesTex Repeated complaints about suspense and guesses about a symbolic launch time reflected the launch atmosphere, not confirmed scheduling information. @teortaxesTex , @teortaxesTex , @teortaxesTex Architecturally, 104B active parameters do not make this equivalent to storing a 104B dense model : deployment must accommodate the much larger expert pool, plus runtime state. As an illustrative calculation—not a measured configuration—2.8T parameters alone imply approximately 5.6 TB at 16-bit or 1.4 TB at 4-bit , before quantization metadata and serving overhead. The supplied posts disclose no layer layout, expert routing configuration, attention design, training-compute budget, or measured full-context serving footprint. That matters for the “local model” narrative. One enthusiastic post called it Fable 5.1 intelligence available locally, then corrected that weights would arrive November 4. Separately, @giffmana warned against calling trillion-parameter models “local” when deployment requires substantial accelerator infrastructure. Self-hostable and consumer-device-local are different properties
